Yumi Language Guide

This guide is a tour of what Yumi can do, for readers deciding whether they want to try it. Each chapter introduces a capability, shows what it looks like, and explains the choices it opens up. It assumes familiarity with programming, but not with Yumi.

The language

  1. Yumi at a glance — The ideas that come together in the language.
  2. Syntax and expressions — Reading the notation; expression functions, lazy bindings, and expressive calls.
  3. String templates — Text-producing functions, interpolation, composition, and multiline documents.
  4. The type system — Static typing, inference, optionals, generics, narrowing, and conversions.
  5. Classes, interfaces, and dispatch — Objects, tuples, inheritance, delegation, and overloading.
  6. Sum types and enums — Modeling alternatives and the data that belongs to each case.
  7. Structural pattern matching and destructuring — Recognizing a value's shape and giving its parts names.
  8. Numerical units — Unit literals, conversions, arithmetic, and percentages.
  9. Collections and data layout — Lists, maps, arrays, views, bitmaps, and tables.
  10. Streams — A common model for stored, generated, and arriving values.
  11. Stream pipelines — Constructing sequences and composing transformations.
  12. Stream pattern matching — Grammars over text, bytes, and other sequences.
  13. Concurrency and reactivity — Tasks, channels, events, and expressions that follow changing state.
  14. State machines — Named states, event-driven transitions, payloads, and state-owned lifetimes.
  15. Errors — Automatic propagation, recovery, panics, and cleanup.
  16. Markup and stylesheets — Declarative object trees, composition, styling, and live state.
  17. Modules, native code, and memory — Program organization, compilation, C interoperability, and memory control.
  18. Probes and observability — Observing execution, values, and object state.
  19. Batteries included — A tour of the standard library's capabilities.

The reasoning behind Yumi

  1. Why Yumi looks the way it does — Unusual syntax choices, alternatives, and tradeoffs.
  2. Features you may not like — Deliberate choices that may influence whether Yumi appeals to you.

Finding your way

Start with Yumi at a glance for the overall picture. The language chapters can then be read in order or by interest. Batteries included answers the practical question of what kinds of programs the supplied libraries help build. The design essays explain the reasoning and tradeoffs behind the features shown throughout the guide.

The chapters give each feature a home. Related chapters introduce the connection and link there for the fuller treatment: Streams explains sources, Stream pipelines explains sequence construction and transformation, and the two pattern chapters distinguish inspecting an existing value from recognizing successive input.

Yumi at a glance

Yumi brings together features that are often associated with different kinds of language: static types and inference, objects and pattern matching, lazy expressions and imperative procedures, native code and garbage collection, grammars and declarative interfaces.

Its central attraction is the way these features meet. A stream can contain numbers already in memory or characters arriving from a socket. A pattern can turn those characters into records. A pipeline can transform the records, and a live expression can expose the latest result to an interface. Each step can use the form that expresses its own job clearly.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Describe valuesStatic types, inference, tuples, classes, interfaces, unions, and numerical units.
Transform sequencesOne stream family for stored collections, generators, channels, and publications.
Recognize inputStructural patterns for values; stream grammars for successive items.
Coordinate workTasks, channels, ordinary calls that can wait, and automatic error propagation.
Build interfacesMarkup, styles, events, and expressions that follow changing state.
Reach the machineNative compilation, a C bridge, managed memory, and explicit storage choices.

Start with the result

Yumi often puts the answer first and its supporting calculations below it:

  • Answer first: The body describes the returned text; no explicit return is needed.
  • Name a dependency: A lazy binding explains how the text is assembled.
  • Filter and transform: Keep odd inputs and square them. The call prints Squares of odd values: 9, 25.
-- summary([2, 3, 4, 5])

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ summary
    - values [Int]

"Squares of odd values: $text"

.. text = ", ".join(squares)
.. squares = each * each in values when each % 2 != 0

The notation is intentionally distinctive. Dividers separate declarations, identifiers use kebab case, types begin with capitals, and several common operations have symbolic forms. After the initial adjustment, these conventions make declarations and operations visually recognizable. Syntax and expressions introduces that vocabulary.

Choose a model that fits the data

ModelUse it to describe
Classes and interfacesState, behavior, and shared capabilities
Tuples and unionsValues with several fields, or alternatives with different payloads
Numerical unitsQuantities whose types carry their meaning
Generic typesOperations that preserve relationships across concrete types

These choices work with static typing, but a program need not repeat every type that the compiler can infer. Generics let an operation work across types while retaining the information it needs. Pattern matching can use that information to recognize and unpack values.

A completed download, for example, can carry a path as part of its union case. A duration can carry its unit in its type. Neither requires relying on a comment to explain what a bare string or number is supposed to mean.

Sequences connect stored data and ongoing work

The stream family accepts multiple representations of successive values. Consumers can work over collections, generators, channels, and broadcasters. The operation can be written once even when some sources must wait for their next item.

  • Stream pipelines assemble, filter, and transform sequences.
  • Stream patterns recognize sequences using grammar rules.
  • Structural patterns inspect tuples, maps, lists, and other values.

Waiting can pass through ordinary functions

An operation that waits for IO does not force every enclosing function to acquire an async declaration or every call to acquire await. Tasks make concurrency explicit; ordinary calls can still suspend the task performing them.

This keeps helper functions easy to compose, while making timing something the reader must understand from an operation's behavior. Recoverable errors similarly propagate through calls until a caller chooses to handle them. These choices reduce ceremony and also move some responsibility into the design of APIs and their documentation.

Interfaces are part of the language story

Yumi has markup for object trees, stylesheets, events, and tracked values. These are useful for interfaces whose appearance and content follow application state. The supplied terminal and graphical libraries provide concrete components on top of those language features.

The standard library reaches beyond interfaces: it includes networking, structured data, files and storage, time, graphics, AI integrations, and language tooling. The Batteries included chapter surveys those capabilities.

High-level code with a native foundation

Yumi compiles to native code and provides a C bridge. Garbage collection is the normal memory model, while arrays, tables, explicit backing storage, and lower-level memory facilities provide more control where representation matters. Probes make observations about execution part of the language's tooling story.

The guide explores these capabilities without assuming that every reader wants all of them. For the deliberate compromises behind the design, start with Features you may not like. For the notation itself, read Why Yumi looks the way it does.

Syntax and expressions

Yumi's syntax gives the shape of a program a visible vocabulary. Dividers identify boundaries, capitalization helps distinguish types from values, and symbols mark operations such as return, yield, matching, and stream transformation. Expression functions and lazy bindings let code begin with the result it is trying to describe.

The details become easier to read together than in isolation. This chapter introduces the forms that recur throughout the guide; the syntax essay explains their design tradeoffs.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Declaration boundariesThick dividers separate top-level declarations; thin dividers separate members.
Names and spacingdisplay-name is a value name; DisplayName is a type; a - b is subtraction.
Expression functionsState the answer, then explain its lazy dependencies with ...
Proceduresdo gives ordered steps, mutation, loops, and explicit returns.
Calls and textNamed arguments, function values, interpolation, and ¶ templates.

Declarations have visible boundaries

  • New declaration: The thick divider establishes a top-level boundary.
  • Public name: + exposes the declaration.
  • Parameter: The indented line names an input and its type.
  • Flush-left body: The expression supplies the result. Thin dividers separate members inside a type.
-- greeting("Ada")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ greeting
    - name String

"Hello, $name"

Indentation groups nested code, but function bodies begin flush to the left. This gives a function a distinctive silhouette: its name and parameter block above, its work below. Dividers are part of the syntax rather than optional visual decoration.

Types such as String begin with a capital. Ordinary names such as display-name use lowercase kebab case. Whitespace separates operators from their operands, keeping subtraction distinct from the hyphens in names: starting-count - removed-count.

An expression can be the whole function

-- doubled(21)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ doubled
    - value Int

value * 2
  • Result expression: The body is the answer; the call produces 42. A conditional, match, pipeline, or text expression can occupy the same position.

For example, a decision can be written as a table of expressions:

-- stock-label(2)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ stock-label
    - count Int

match count
    |= 0
        "Empty"
    |? it < 3
        "Low"
    ??
        "Available"
  • Value arm: Zero selects "Empty".
  • Predicate arm: The next test selects "Low" for this call.
  • Fallback: Every remaining value produces "Available"; the selected arm supplies the function result.

Lazy bindings put dependencies below the result

.. introduces a lazy binding. A function can use a name before the binding appears in its source, so its main expression can stay at the top:

  • Document first: The output uses total before its binding appears in the source.
  • Lazy calculation: The initializer runs when its value is needed. An unused dependency need not run.
-- receipt-line("Apples", 3, 2)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ receipt-line
    - label String
    - quantity Int
    - price Int

"$label: $quantity for $total"

.. total = quantity * price

Evaluation timing matters if an initializer performs IO or changes state. A lazy binding is not a decorative synonym for an ordinary assignment. Likewise, it does not by itself mean that a result automatically stays synchronized with changing inputs. Tracked dependencies and live expressions are covered in Concurrency and reactivity.

Procedures make state changes explicit

Yumi also supports ordinary local variables, loops, mutation, and early exits. A do function provides an imperative body:

-- total([1, 2, 3])

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do total
    - values [Int]

. result = 0
for value in values
    result += value
= result
  • Procedure: do introduces a body of ordered steps.
  • Local state: . creates a variable that the loop updates.
  • Explicit return: = supplies the answer. Procedures and expression functions can call each other.

Yumi uses related symbols for other control-flow operations. <= yields one item from a generator, <<= yields the items of another source, and ?! signals an error or panic. Their fuller contracts belong to Streams and Errors.

Calls can name relationships

An ordinary call uses parentheses, as in greeting("Ada"). A longer call can place one argument on each line. A bullet passes an argument by its parameter's name, making its role part of the call's wording.

This fragment declares the parameters and calls the function by name:

-- distance • from origin • to destination

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ distance
    - from Point
    - to Point
  • Source relationship: from names the argument at the call site and in the body.
  • Destination relationship: The call reads distance • from origin • to destination.

Named infix operators offer another way to express a relationship between operands. Together with operator overloading, they let domain operations participate in expressions. Their value depends on restraint: an unfamiliar name should make the relationship clearer, and its behavior should remain discoverable.

Functions can be values

An operation can accept a function, retain it, or return one. Short expression functions can be written inline; this fragment supplies a two-argument addition function:

:: total, item => total + item
  • Inputs: The inline function accepts two values.
  • Answer: The expression after => computes their sum.

Stream stages have a convenient per-item name, each, so a transformation can read values *> each * 2. Calling a function in such a stage still requires a call expression. *> double(each) invokes double; *> double produces the function value.

Text can have the shape of its output

Strings support interpolation, as the earlier examples show. Larger text can use a template body, introduced with ¶:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ page String
    - title String
    - body String

<html>
    <head><title>$title</title></head>
    <body>$body</body>
</html>
  • Template function: ¶ makes the body text that produces a string.
  • Interpolation: Values are inserted into the text using ordinary Yumi expressions.

This is text construction. Markup is a separate capability that constructs object trees. Both let the source resemble the structure of the result, but they produce different kinds of value.

See String templates for interpolation, supporting calculations, conditional content, repetition, composition, and whitespace.

That is the recurring theme of the syntax: expressions for answers, patterns for shapes, pipelines for sequences, and markup for trees. The language offers procedural control too; the useful choice is the form that makes the current operation easiest to see.

String templates

A string template function lets its body look like the text it produces. The declaration begins with ¶, followed by the function's name and ordinary parameters. After the signature, the body is text with embedded Yumi expressions.

This is useful for messages, documents, reports, and generated source. The surrounding text remains readable as a whole, while the changing parts come from the same functions, types, and expressions used elsewhere in the program.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
¶ functionWrite a multiline document as the body of a function returning text.
$name, ${expression}Insert values and calculations from ordinary Yumi code.
════════════════════End literal text and define supporting calculations below it.
Conditions and repetitionUse conditional expressions, matches, comprehensions, and join.
CompositionCall templates from templates, or define a type's string converter.
Output contractWhitespace and escaping belong to the document format you are producing.

Text as a function body

  • Text function: ¶ appears before the function name; no outer quotes or explicit return are needed.
  • Ordinary input: The template accepts parameters like any other function.
  • Two paragraphs: The call inserts Ada and returns the text. The caller chooses whether to print, save, or send it.
-- greeting("Ada")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ greeting
    - name String

Hello, $name.

Welcome to Yumi.

A short message may fit comfortably in an ordinary quoted string. The template form becomes more useful as the text acquires lines, indentation, punctuation, and repeated structure.

Interpolation uses Yumi expressions

$name inserts a named value. ${expression} inserts the result of an expression:

-- line-item("Apples", 3, 2)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ line-item
    - name String
    - quantity Int
    - price Int

$name: $quantity at $price each, total ${quantity * price}
  • Named value: Insert an input directly.
  • Expression: Compute the total using ordinary arithmetic. Numbers participate in string construction without a separate template evaluator.

Simple property access can use forms such as $person.name. Braces are useful for more substantial expressions and for making the boundary between a name and adjacent text explicit. For example, ${name}-report clearly places the hyphenated suffix outside the identifier.

Quotation marks can appear directly in the text body. Interpolation and escape sequences still have meaning: \$name produces the literal text $name, and \\ represents a literal backslash. The template frees the document from outer quotes without turning it into an entirely uninterpreted block of bytes.

Put the document first, then its dependencies

A larger template can name its supporting calculations below the text. The double-line divider ends the text portion while keeping the following code inside the function:

  • Document: The main expression shows the receipt before its calculations.
  • Back to code: The double-line divider ends text within this function.
  • Dependency: The lazy binding supplies the value used by $total.
-- receipt("Apples", 3, 2)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ receipt
    - name String
    - quantity Int
    - price Int

Receipt
=======
Item: $name
Quantity: $quantity
Total: $total

════════════════════
.. total = quantity * price

This is the same result-first organization available to expression functions. It also gives calculations a place to grow without making every interpolation harder to read. A lookup, a match, or a sequence operation can live in a named dependency while the template continues to show the document's structure.

The dividers have different jobs. ════════════════════ returns from text to code within the current function. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ introduces the next top-level declaration. Without the text-ending boundary, a line that looks like a calculation is still part of the template's text.

Conditional content

Conditional text can use an ordinary conditional expression. There is no need to introduce a second set of template-specific decision rules:

-- heading("Release notes", true)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ heading
    - title String
    - is-draft Bool

# $title$suffix

════════════════════
.. suffix = if is-draft then " (draft)" else ""
  • Placement: The literal body describes where the optional wording belongs.
  • Decision: The choice gives the wording or an empty string.

For a larger decision, the dependency can be a match whose branches return text, including calls to other template functions. A whole section can therefore vary while the surrounding document remains in one place.

This keeps the responsibility clear: the expression chooses the content, and the template places that content in the document. A line containing the word if in the literal body does not begin a conditional statement.

Repetition and composition

A template can call another template just as it calls any other function. Repetition can come from a comprehension or stream pipeline, with join choosing the separator:

  • Insert the rows: The outer template owns the document.
  • Separate the results: The join puts a newline between items.
  • Repeat an ordinary call: The comprehension calls the item template once per input.
  • Reusable piece: The inner template owns one item's presentation and remains independently callable.
-- shopping-list(["Apples", "Pears", "Bread"])

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ shopping-list
    - items [String]

Shopping list
=============
$rows

════════════════════
.. rows = "\n".join(lines)
.. lines = shopping-item(each) in items

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ shopping-item
    - item String

- $item

The same arrangement scales to a report containing sections, a message containing optional details, or generated source containing repeated declarations. Each piece remains callable on its own and can receive the data it needs through ordinary parameters.

A collection or stream supplies the sequence; the template does not need its own collection model. Stream pipelines can filter or transform the input before it becomes text. Joining a sequence into one string does need the sequence to finish, so an ongoing source needs a meaningful boundary before it can become a complete document.

Whitespace belongs to the result

Within the text body, indentation is text indentation rather than nested Yumi code:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ¶ outline

Project
    Documentation
        Language guide
    Examples
  • Text indentation: These spaces and internal newlines belong to the result, rather than creating nested Yumi blocks.

Internal newlines, blank lines, and indentation let the source express the layout of the output. The blank line after the signature introduces the body; it is not an extra opening paragraph. Trailing literal whitespace at the end of the template is trimmed, which keeps spacing before a declaration boundary out of the result.

When a final newline is part of the intended output, express it as content rather than relying on blank source lines at the boundary. For example, a final ${"\n"} inserts a newline as an expression result.

Composition also makes whitespace a deliberate choice. A child template returns its text; interpolating it does not automatically reindent all of its lines to match the insertion point. A join's separator and any indentation inside the child are part of the resulting document. This is especially useful to keep in mind when producing nested source code or other indentation-sensitive formats.

Templates can define a type's text form

The template form also works for a string converter inside a type:

. entry = Entry("Apples", 3)
-- entry as String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Entry is Tuple

+ name String
+ quantity Int

────────────────────
+ ¶ to String

$name × $quantity
  • Request text: The cast invokes the type's string conversion.
  • Template converter: A type member can define text with the same syntax as a free function.
  • Read fields: The converter uses the value's fields; this produces Apples × 3.

A value may need several representations, however. A short label, a detailed report, and a serialized record can have different purposes. Named template functions let those choices remain explicit rather than making one string conversion serve every caller.

Text generation and structured output

Templates can produce Markdown, HTML, configuration, or source code because their output is text. They do not infer the escaping rules of the format from what that text resembles. An interpolation into HTML, JSON, or another format needs the conversion appropriate to that position. The JSON library, for example, performs escaping explicitly when constructing a quoted JSON string.

For data serialization, a format library can own that contract. For a document whose wording and arrangement are the main concern, a template keeps the authored text visible. These approaches can compose: an embedded value can come from a serializer or a formatting helper.

String templates and markup

A template containing <Box> produces text containing those characters. Markup constructs a tree of objects with properties, children, events, and lifetimes. That difference determines which feature fits the result.

Desired resultChoose
Email, report, prompt, generated fileA string template
Data encoded for a protocolA format library that owns serialization and escaping
Live object tree with events and propertiesMarkup
A component containing longer textMarkup whose property calls a template

String template functions bring text into the same compositional model as other Yumi code. Parameters describe the inputs, expressions compute the changing parts, and function calls assemble larger results. The body remains a document that a reader can recognize.

The type system

Yumi is statically typed, but it leaves much of the repetition out of the source. The compiler can infer types from initializers, function bodies, and calls. Explicit types remain useful when they explain a domain boundary or choose among possible representations.

The type system is also a way to describe meaning. A value can be optional, a choice between named alternatives, a number with a unit, or an object offering a particular interface. Generics let operations preserve those distinctions while working across concrete types.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
InferenceOmit information the compiler can establish; keep explicit types for meaningful boundaries.
OptionalsT? describes presence or absence; ?? supplies a fallback.
GenericsList'Int, [Int], and <Int> preserve item-type information.
AlternativesUnions model domain choices; Or families accept several source types.
ConversionsTypes can adapt values implicitly or through an explicit as expression.

Inference and explicit intent

  • Inferred locals: Initializers supply the types.
  • Explicit representation: The declaration chooses a wider integer. Function results and, with sufficient context, parameters can also be inferred.
. count = 3
. title = "Report"
. total I64 = count
-- "$title: $total"

Inference does not make a value dynamically typed. An operation still needs a suitable implementation for the types involved. The source simply does not have to spell out every piece of information the compiler can establish.

That flexibility is particularly useful for small helpers. Explicit parameter types become more valuable when a signature is meant to communicate a stable contract to other readers.

Absence is represented in the type

An optional type adds the possibility that a value is absent:

. nickname String?
-- nickname ?? "Anonymous"
  • Optional type: A string may be present or absent. An empty string is still present.
  • Fallback: Use the nickname when present, otherwise "Anonymous".

A conditional expression can produce an optional value, and match? can return an optional result when only some shapes matter. This lets absence flow through an expression without inventing a sentinel such as an empty string or a negative number.

The force operator ! asserts that an optional is present. It is useful when a stronger invariant exists, but it transfers responsibility to the author. Where absence is ordinary, a fallback, branch, or optional match says more about the intended behavior.

Absence is also distinct from a recoverable error. A lookup can reasonably find nothing; a network request can fail to obtain an answer. Errors explains the separate failure channel and its automatic propagation.

Generics preserve useful information

Apostrophes attach type arguments to parameterized types: List'Int is a list of integers, and Map'String'Int maps strings to integers. Familiar shapes have shorthand, including [Int] for a list and <Int> for the stream family.

A generic function can keep its item type while accepting different inputs:

  • Different callers: One call produces integers, the other characters.
  • Type parameter: Item connects the input type to the yielded values.
  • Source family: Accept any supported stream representation without converting every item to a common boxed value.
-- List(twice([1, 2]))
-- List(twice("ab"))

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do twice'Item
    - values <Item>

for value in values
    <= value
    <= value

Generic constraints let a declaration require a capability or a type family. The important question is what the implementation needs: indexing, arithmetic, comparison, iteration, or some domain-specific interface. Generics are most useful when that requirement stays smaller than a particular implementation's complete API.

Alternatives have more than one role

A union describes a value with alternatives. It can name cases and attach data to them, as in a response that is either pending or complete. An Or type describes an accepted family of types. The stream declaration is an important example:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Stream'T is CursorIterable'T || Indexable'T || Iterable'T || Broadcastable'T || ImmutableArray'T
  • Accepted alternatives: The family joins supported ways to obtain items. It does not introduce named domain states such as Download.pending.

This allows a stream-oriented function to accept sources with different iteration mechanisms. It is a different purpose from introducing named domain states such as Download.pending. The Sum types and Streams chapters show those two uses in context.

Interfaces provide another form of generality: an operation asks for a capability that multiple types can implement. Choosing among an interface, a union, and an accepted type family depends on whether the program is describing shared behavior, distinct alternatives, or supported inputs.

Matching refines what is known

A type test or pattern can establish more specific information about a value. Inside a branch for one union case, the program can use the payload that belongs to that case. A nested pattern can recognize a map entry whose value is a particular kind of collection.

The useful consequence is local clarity. A branch can operate on the value its condition established, rather than repeat casts and defensive checks. See Structural pattern matching for recognition and extraction.

Conversions are part of composition

Yumi permits implicit conversions, including numeric conversions, and types can define their own conversion behavior. as makes a requested conversion explicit. A conversion can make a domain value usable as text or adapt a source to an interface expected by a consumer.

Implicit conversion is convenient, but it is not a universal promise of losslessness. Numeric narrowing can change a value's representation; domain conversions can perform meaningful work. A signature and its conversions should make the interpretation of an input predictable.

Numerical units shows a particularly useful application: different numeric representations remain connected by declared unit relationships. The types participate in ordinary expressions while preserving more meaning than a bare machine number would carry.

What the types buy

The attraction is a combination of concise code and expressive contracts. A function can avoid obvious annotations while still describing absence, capabilities, alternatives, or units at its boundary. Those distinctions help both the compiler and the person reading the program.

Inference, conversions, and dispatch also mean that understanding a difficult call may require looking beyond its local spelling. Yumi accepts that tradeoff; the guide's design discussion considers it directly.

Classes, interfaces, and dispatch

Yumi supports object-oriented programming alongside tuples, unions, and generic functions. Classes can own state and behavior, interfaces describe capabilities, and dispatch selects an implementation suited to the values involved in a call.

The interesting choice is how much structure a problem needs. Some data is naturally a tuple. Some behavior belongs to an object with identity and a lifetime. Some operations describe a relationship between several types and fit better as overloaded functions.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
TupleGroup value fields and give them behavior.
ClassModel identity, changing state, and virtual methods.
InterfaceAsk for a capability without choosing its implementation.
Inheritance / delegationShare a base implementation, or forward behavior to a contained value.
Dispatch / operators / extensionsDefine operations around the types and relationships involved.

Data can carry behavior

  • Value type: Point represents a small value whose meaning comes from its contents.
  • Shared shape: Every point contains two coordinates.
  • Behavior: The method reads those fields; the call produces (3, 4).
. point = Point(3, 4)
-- point.label()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Point is Tuple

+ x Int
+ y Int

────────────────────
+ label

"($x, $y)"

Yumi also provides structs and explicit collection layouts. The representation question is covered further in Collections and data layout; a type's methods and its storage needs are related decisions, but they are not the same decision.

Objects can own changing state

  • Stored state: The object owns the counter.
  • Changing behavior: advance updates the field, so the subsequent read prints 1.
. counter = Counter()
counter.advance()
-- counter.count

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Counter

+ count Int

────────────────────
+ do advance

count += 1

The object owns the counter and exposes an operation that changes it. Constructors use the name This, and a type can provide constructors appropriate to different inputs. Properties can expose stored data or computed getters; their syntax lets callers read a value through the same property access form.

That convenience makes API design important. A property read should have a sensible cost and effect model for the object it belongs to. A getter is not automatically a field access, and an object's public properties need not expose its complete internal representation.

Constructors initialize fields with ..

. log = Log("build")
-- log.lines.length, log.title

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Log

+ title String
+ lines [String]

────────────────────
+ This
    - name String

lines += "started $name"
title = name

.. lines = List'String()

A .. line in a constructor that names a field gives the field its starting value. It replaces the field's declared default, so the default is never built. Every such initializer runs once, before the first statement of the constructor body, wherever it is written. The body then reads and writes the field itself, so lines above already holds a list when the body appends to it.

An initializer can read constructor parameters and other fields. It cannot read a field that the constructor body assigns: the initializer would see the value from before the assignment, so the compiler rejects it.

Interfaces describe a capability

-- describe(Label("Ready"))

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Described is Interface

────────────────────
+ description String

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Label is Tuple
    is Described

+ text String

────────────────────
+ description

text

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe
    - value Described

value.description()
  • Contract: The interface requires a description.
  • Implementation: Label supplies the capability using its stored text.
  • Consumer boundary: describe needs the capability, not the concrete class. Other implementations can carry different state.

This is useful at boundaries where callers need a small capability. A renderer may need something drawable; a stream consumer needs a supported way to obtain items. Neither should necessarily depend on one concrete storage or implementation choice.

An interface value can be narrowed back to a concrete implementer with is, as, or a match type pattern, and the test also accepts subclasses of the named class. Argument dispatch never narrows implicitly: a function that takes a concrete class does not accept an interface value.

An interface can declare using SomeStyle. Style reads such as value.$fill and imperative style writes such as value.fill = paint then work directly on interface values, and every implementing class must use the same styles.

Inheritance and virtual methods

A class can derive from another class, share its behavior, and override methods. Calls through the base type can then reach an implementation supplied by the actual object.

Inside a class's methods, This names the class that declares them, the same type this has there. A subclass inherits those methods as written, so a base method that returns This returns the base type even when it is called on a subclass.

  • Useful when: a family shares a conceptual identity and useful behavior.
  • Cost: subclasses depend on decisions in the base class.
  • Contract: overrides should preserve callers' expectations about effects, assumptions, and cost.

An interface can express common behavior without requiring the same class hierarchy. A union can express a closed set of alternatives when callers should consider each case explicitly. Yumi supplies all three approaches; Sum types shows the latter in detail.

Delegation makes composition convenient

An object can contain another value and expose selected behavior through it. Yumi has declaration syntax for forwarding interfaces to stored members. A stream wrapper, for example, can expose a readable capability through its input member and a writable capability through a different output member.

This reduces repetitive forwarding methods while keeping the ownership structure visible: the enclosing object has an implementation it uses, rather than needing to inherit all of that implementation's identity. The wrapper can still add its own state and operations.

Delegation also raises a lifetime question. Forwarding a capability does not by itself say whether the outer object owns the delegated resource, shares it, or merely borrows access. That relationship belongs in the component's contract.

More than one argument can select behavior

Overloaded functions allow implementations specialized for different parameter types. Multiple dispatch makes the types of several arguments relevant, rather than requiring every operation to be organized around one distinguished receiver.

For geometry, the relationship can select the algorithm:

Inputs to an intersection operationImplementation needed
Line and lineLine intersection
Line and curveLine–curve intersection
Curve and curveCurve intersection

The combinations can share one operation name. See the overload example for the declaration shape.

This can be more direct than asking one object to discover the second object's type and manually branch. It also makes the set of available overloads part of understanding a call. Ambiguous or overly broad definitions can make that set harder to reason about.

Operators and extensions

Operators can be implemented by types. Adding two vectors or comparing two domain values can therefore use ordinary expression syntax. Named infix operators offer a readable name when the relationship does not fit a familiar symbol.

Extensions let behavior be declared outside the original type body. This is useful when an operation belongs to a library's use of a type, rather than to the type's original definition. Alongside conversions and overloads, extensions give libraries room to integrate with existing values without requiring every integration to be built into the base class.

The benefit is expressive composition. The cost is that an expression's meaning may depend on declarations elsewhere in the program. Good names, focused interfaces, and restrained overloading make that tradeoff easier to live with.

Sum types

A sum type describes a value that can be one of several alternatives. A download might be waiting, in progress, or complete. Each alternative can carry the data that belongs to it: progress needs a byte count, while completion needs the downloaded file's path.

A value holds one active case together with its associated data, also called its payload.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Named union casesDistinguish domain states and give each its own payload.
Type alternativesUse existing types as the distinctions in a union.
Anonymous casesInfer local alternatives from expressions such as ..accepted(name).
Matches and testsHandle cases together with match, or narrow one branch with is.
EnumsName particular values that share one class's representation and behavior.

A value with alternatives

Yumi calls these types unions. Declare one with is Union, then list its cases with |:

  • Construct a state: Choose the completed case and supply its path.
  • Read its payload: The arm binds the path and prints Saved to report.pdf.
  • No payload: Waiting needs no extra data.
  • Several fields: Progress carries both byte counts.
  • One field: A completed download carries its path as part of construction.
. download = Download.complete("report.pdf")
-- match download
    | .waiting
        "Waiting"
    | .progress(received, total)
        "$received of $total bytes"
    | .complete(path)
        "Saved to $path"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Download is Union

| waiting
| progress(received Int, total Int)
| complete(path String)

Declaring and constructing cases

A case can have no payload, a single payload type, or a tuple of named fields. These declaration fragments illustrate the forms:

| waiting
| complete String
| progress(received Int, total Int)

Construct a case through its union type. A case without data is a value such as Download.waiting. A case with data takes arguments, as in Download.complete("report.pdf") or Download.progress(20, 100).

Case names preserve distinctions that the payload type alone cannot express. For example, a horizontal move and a vertical move can both carry an integer:

. move = Move.vertical(12)
-- match move
    | .horizontal(distance)
        "Across $distance"
    | .vertical(distance)
        "Down $distance"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Move is Union

| horizontal Int
| vertical Int
  • Choose by name: Both alternatives carry Int; the constructor says which meaning applies.
  • Distinct roles: A shared payload type does not collapse the cases. The match prints Down 12.

Matching cases

The patterns in this chapter are part of Yumi's broader structural pattern matching and destructuring vocabulary. Here the focus is how those patterns work with a union's alternatives.

match selects behavior according to the active case. A pattern such as .complete(path) checks the case and binds its payload to a local name. A tuple pattern such as .progress(received, total) binds the individual fields. The names in the pattern are chosen by the match; they do not have to repeat the field names in the declaration.

The leading dot in these patterns lets Yumi resolve the case against the subject's type. You can also qualify the case, as in Download.complete(path), when spelling out the type makes the code clearer.

An ordinary match over a union must cover all its cases. Omitting a case is a compile error, even when the value was just constructed using one of the cases that you did handle. This keeps the match tied to the full type's possibilities.

A ?? fallback can handle the remaining cases. Prefer explicit cases when adding a new alternative should force callers to reconsider their behavior; use a fallback when the remaining cases deliberately share one answer.

When an unmatched case should produce no value, use match?:

. download = Download.waiting
. path = match? download
    | .complete(path)
        path
-- path ?? "No file yet"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Download is Union

| waiting
| complete(path String)
  • Partial interest: Return a path only when the completed case matches.
  • Handle absence: The waiting case produces no value, so this prints No file yet.

Testing and narrowing

Use is when you only need to test a case. Within a branch established by that test, Yumi can narrow the value to the case's payload:

. event = Event.click(10, 20)
if event is .click
    -- event.x
    -- event.y

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Event is Union

| click(x Int, y Int)
| key String
  • Establish the case: The test narrows event inside the branch.
  • Use the payload: The narrowed value exposes the click fields, printing 10 and 20.

Comparing with == or != against a case that carries no payload, such as Fill.none or .none, narrows the same way as is. Ruling out each payload-free case leaves the remaining case, so a chain that handles inherit and none first can use the payload in its final branch. A comparison with a case that holds a value stays an ordinary value comparison and does not narrow.

Narrowing is useful for a focused check. Matching is useful when the alternatives together form the decision you want to express.

Named cases also expose payload accessors, such as download.complete. These accessors do not prove that the case is active: in the current implementation, an accessor for an inactive case returns the payload type's default value. Use a case test or a match when the distinction matters. For example, an empty string by itself cannot tell you whether a string case was active.

Alternatives identified by type

A union can list existing types directly, without introducing case names:

  • Enter the union: The string converts to the corresponding alternative.
  • Match by type: Capture the string directly; the result is Text hello.
  • Existing distinctions: The types themselves identify the alternatives.
. value NumberOrText = "hello"
-- match value
    | number Int
        "Number $number"
    | text String
        "Text $text"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ NumberOrText is Union

| Int
| String

Use this form when the existing types already communicate the distinction. Use named cases when the distinction belongs to your domain, particularly when different cases carry the same type. The two styles can coexist in one union. For example, the standard library's Fill combines named inherit, none, and stroke cases with RGBA and FillStack type alternatives.

An explicit cast can extract a type alternative, but a cast to an inactive alternative raises an error. A match makes the alternatives and their handling visible in one place.

Anonymous cases

Some decisions need several possible outcomes without needing a separately declared type. Yumi can infer an anonymous union from case expressions written with two leading dots:

-- describe(check-name("Yumi"))
-- describe(check-name(""))

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ check-name
    - name String

|? name.length > 0
    ..accepted(name)
??
    ..empty

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ describe String
    - result

match result
    | .accepted(name)
        "Hello, $name"
    | .empty
        "Enter a name"
  • Infer a payload case: This outcome contributes an accepted case with a string payload.
  • Infer an empty case: This outcome carries no payload.
  • Match normally: The caller uses a single-dot case pattern. The calls print Hello, Yumi and Enter a name.

The punctuation distinguishes introducing an inferred case with ..accepted from referring to an existing case with .accepted. Anonymous cases need a stable owner for the inferred result, such as a function result or a bound variable. They cannot be introduced in every arbitrary expression position. Repeated uses of the same inferred case name must also agree on their number of payload arguments.

Anonymous cases are convenient for local decisions and inferred return values. A declared union gives a shared concept an explicit name and a single place to define its alternatives.

Behavior on a union

A union can define methods alongside its cases. This is useful when callers should ask the value for an answer instead of repeating the same match:

-- Download.waiting.label()
-- Download.complete("report.pdf").label()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Download is Union

| waiting
| complete(path String)

────────────────────
+ label String

match this
    | .waiting
        "Waiting"
    | .complete(path)
        "Saved to $path"
  • Shared operation: Callers ask every case for a label.
  • Decision inside the type: The method owns the case analysis. The calls print Waiting and Saved to report.pdf.

Related feature: enums

Yumi also uses | declarations to give names to particular values of a class. These are enum members. They share the enclosing class's representation and behavior, and they can be more than integer constants.

The simplest numeric form lists names inside an integer-based class:

  • Numeric class: Priority supplies the representation; there is no separate enum keyword.
  • Named values: Implicit values start at zero. These members print 0, 1, and 2.
-- Priority.low
-- Priority.normal
-- Priority.high

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Priority is Int

| low
| normal
| high

Explicit values

Use = to supply a member's value. This is useful when the numbers have meaning outside the declaration, such as protocol codes:

. code = ResponseCode.not-found
-- code
-- match code
    |= ResponseCode.ok
        "Found"
    |= ResponseCode.not-found
        "Missing"
    ??
        "Other response"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ ResponseCode is Int

| ok = 200
| not-found = 404
  • External meaning: Assign the numeric value required by the protocol.
  • Value match: |= compares against the member; it does not extract a union payload. The output is 404, then Missing.

Enum members are matched as values with |=. A union pattern such as | .complete(path) checks a case and extracts its payload; an enum arm such as |= ResponseCode.ok compares against the named value. When the subject supplies the type, the shorter |= .ok form is also available.

Members with shared data

Enum members can be instances of a tuple or an ordinary class. Each member then has the same fields, initialized with its own values:

  • Shared fields: Every member has the same field layout; no case test is needed before reading it.
  • Member data: Each named value initializes that layout. The calls print North, 1, and Go east.
-- Direction.north.label
-- Direction.east.dx
-- match Direction.east
    |= Direction.north
        "Go north"
    |= Direction.east
        "Go east"
    ??
        "Other direction"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Direction is (dx Int, dy Int, label String)

| north = (0, -1, "North")
| east = (1, 0, "East")

For an ordinary class, member initializers use the class's construction and conversion behavior. The enum declaration does not invent fields from the initializer. Define the fields and any constructor the class needs, just as for other instances.

The standard library uses this feature for calendar values. DayOfWeek members carry full and abbreviated names, while Month members carry names, a month number, and a day count. Methods and conversions on their enclosing types operate on that shared data.

Enums and unions

Both features give alternatives readable names, but their declarations describe different things:

FeatureWhat the names describeWhere the data is defined
Enum membersParticular values of one classShared fields or numeric representation on the class
Union casesAlternatives that a union value can holdA separate payload shape for each case

An enum member such as Direction.east comes with its declared field values. A union constructor such as Download.progress(20, 100) creates a case value with data supplied by the caller.

Use enums for named values with a common shape: priorities, protocol codes, or calendar entries with shared metadata. Use unions when the alternatives need different data or represent distinct roles for the same payload type. A union containing only cases without payloads is also useful for a set of named choices that does not need a numeric representation or shared fields.

Choosing the alternatives

Start with the states or values the program actually needs to distinguish. Give each case the data required to make it meaningful. Avoid adding fields to every case merely because one case needs them.

An optional type such as String? expresses a simpler choice: a string is present or absent. A union is useful when absence has several meanings, or when each alternative carries different data. A tuple combines its fields; a union chooses among its cases. Combining the two lets a type say both which situation exists and what is known about it.

Structural pattern matching and destructuring

Structural patterns recognize the shape of an existing value and name the parts that matter. The same vocabulary works in multi-arm decisions, optional extraction, Boolean tests, conditional bindings, and destructuring assignments.

The result is less separation between asking a question and using its answer. A branch can say “a click with coordinates x and y” instead of testing a tag, casting a payload, and reading two fields in separate steps.

At a glance

CapabilityFormResult
Choose among shapesmatch valueThe selected arm's value
Extract when possiblematch? valueAn optional result
Test a shapevalue is patternBool
Test and bindif \| pattern = valueNames scoped to the successful branch
Destructure a known shape. pattern = valueNew local bindings
Destructure into variablespattern = valueUpdated existing bindings
Ignore one part_No binding
Capture a remainder...restThe unmatched portion of a collection or text

Patterns can combine literals, types, predicates, tuple positions, union cases, indexed collections, map keys, and text anchors.

A complete example

This function classifies a decoded response while extracting only the data needed by each arm:

  • Literal value pattern: The first arm requires the value at status to equal "ok".
  • Nested collection pattern: The items value must be a nonempty string list. The pattern captures its first item and remainder.
  • Arm result: A match is an expression. The selected arm supplies the function's return value.
  • Exact empty shape: The second arm distinguishes an empty list from a missing or malformed items value.
  • Typed capture: The arm requires a string and binds it as message.
  • Fallback arm: ?? handles every shape not recognized above it.
-- response-summary(response)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ response-summary
    - response [String = Payload]

match response
    | ["status" = "ok", "items" = [first String, ...rest]]
        "First: $first; ${rest.length} more"
    | ["status" = "ok", "items" = []]
        "No items"
    | ["error" = message String]
        "Failed: $message"
    ??
        "Unrecognized response"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Payload is Union

| String
| [String]

The outer map patterns, inner list patterns, literal checks, type checks, captures, and fallback form one decision. Arms are tried in order, so specific shapes should generally precede broader ones.

Pattern building blocks

Patterns can test a value, constrain its type, apply a predicate, or combine those operations with a capture.

PatternMeaning
42Equal to the literal value
StringCompatible with the named type
name StringA string captured as name
{it > 20}Satisfies the predicate
score {it > 20}A value over 20, captured as score
_Any value, without a binding
-- match ("score", 42)
    | label String, amount {it > 20}
        "$label is high: $amount"
    ??
        "No high score"
  • Typed capture: The first tuple field must be a String; the arm names it label.
  • Predicate capture: it is the value being tested. A successful test makes the value available as amount.

For simple decisions, equality and condition arms provide compact alternatives:

match count
    |= 0
        "Empty"
    |? it < 3
        "Almost empty"
    ??
        "Available"
  • |= compares the subject with a value.
  • |? evaluates a condition with the subject available as it.
  • ?? supplies the fallback.

Tuples and union cases

Comma-separated patterns unpack tuple-shaped values positionally. Union-case patterns first select the active case, then unpack its payload.

. event = Event.click(12, 30)
-- match event
    | .click(x, y)
        "Click at $x, $y"
    | .key(text)
        "Key $text"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Event is Union

| click(x Int, y Int)
| key String
  • Union-case pattern: The arm applies only when event contains the click case.
  • Tuple payload: The two payload positions become the local names x and y.
  • Single payload: A one-value case can bind that value directly.

A union match is checked against the type's alternatives. Adding a new case can therefore force exhaustive matches to be reconsidered. See Sum types and enums for the modeling side of this feature.

Tuple-shaped values can be matched without a union case:

-- match (3, 4)
    | x Int, y Int
        x * y

The positions are significant even when the tuple type gives its fields names.

Lists, arrays, and remainders

Bracket patterns recognize supported indexable collections. Without a remainder marker, the length is exact.

PatternAccepted shape
[]Empty
[first, second]Exactly two items
[first, ...]One or more items
[..., last]One or more items, capturing the last
[first, ...rest]A first item plus any remainder
[first, ...middle, last]Two endpoints with any middle
[10, _, ...]Starts with 10 and contains at least two items
. values = Array'Int([10, 20, 30, 40])
. middle = match values
    | [first, ...middle, last]
        middle

-- type-of middle
-- ", ".join(middle)
  • First item: The collection must contain an item at the beginning.
  • Remainder capture: middle receives the slice between the two endpoints.
  • Final item: The pattern also requires and captures an item at the end.

For this array, middle is an Array'Int view containing 20, 30. Remainder captures follow the source's slicing behavior; they do not promise a detached list or copy. Lists, arrays, tables, and other supported indexable values can therefore retain their useful representation.

Strings use text patterns instead of bracket patterns. Streams arriving over time use stream pattern matching.

Maps and nested data

A map pattern requires named keys and applies a pattern to each corresponding value. Extra entries are allowed; ...rest can capture them when they matter.

. settings = Map'String'Int()
settings["width"] = 80
settings["height"] = 24
settings["scale"] = 2

. unused = match settings
    | ["width" = width {it > 0}, "height" = height {it > 0}, ...rest]
        -- "$width by $height"
        rest
  • Required key and predicate: The map must contain a positive value at "width"; that value becomes width.
  • Second required key: A missing or nonpositive height makes the arm fail.
  • Unmatched entries: rest contains entries not consumed by the named key patterns, including "scale" here.

Patterns can nest through maps, lists, tuples, and union-valued fields:

. first = match? response
    | ["choices" = [["message" = message, ...], ...], ...]
        message
  • Nested shape: The pattern requires a choices collection whose first item is a map containing message.

match? returns an absent value when any required layer is missing or has the wrong shape. That makes nested patterns useful for decoded data whose complete schema is larger than the part a caller needs.

Text patterns

Structural text patterns recognize literal anchors and capture the gaps between them.

-- match "name:ada;"
    | "name:" ...name ";"
        name
    ??
        "Invalid record"
  • Literal anchor: The complete string must begin with name:.
  • Captured gap: name receives the text before the next literal anchor.
  • Final anchor: The complete string must end with a semicolon.

The gap may be empty. Structural text patterns allow one remainder, which makes this form suited to a small, anchored text shape. Use stream pattern matching for repetition, character classes, recursive rules, binary decoding, successive records, or input that arrives over time.

Destructuring and conditional binding

When the shape is already expected, a destructuring declaration introduces its parts directly:

. [head, _, ...tail] = [10, 20, 30, 40]
-- head
-- tail
  • Destructuring declaration: head becomes 10, _ ignores 20, and tail becomes [30, 40].

Existing variables can receive destructured values too:

. x = 0
. y = 0
x, y = (10, 20)
-- x + y
  • Destructuring assignment: The tuple's two fields update the existing variables together.

When the shape is uncertain, a conditional binding keeps the extracted names inside the successful branch:

. values = [5, 6, 7, 8]
if | [_, second, ...rest] = values
    -- second
    -- rest
else
    -- "Not enough items"
  • Conditional pattern binding: The condition both tests the shape and introduces second and rest for the branch.

The visual distinction matters: . values [Int] = source binds the entire value with a type annotation, while . [first, ...rest] = source binds parts through a pattern.

Choosing a matching context

The pattern can stay the same while its surrounding form chooses what failure means:

. values = [10, 20, 30]

. optional-head = match? values
    | [head, ...]
        head
  • Optional extraction: A failed pattern produces an absent value rather than selecting another result.
. values = [10, 20, 30]
-- values is [_, _, _]

is answers whether the value has exactly three items.

. values = [10, 20, 30]
do match values
    | [head, ...]
        -- head
    ??
        -- "Empty"
  • Imperative match: do match selects statements instead of producing one expression value.
ContextOn failure
match valueAnother arm, ??, an explicit failure, or a non-exhaustive-match error
match? valueAn absent result
value is patternfalse
if \| pattern = valueThe next branch or else
. pattern = valueThe declared expectation fails
do match? valueImperative execution continues without an arm

Closed domains such as union cases support exhaustiveness checking. An arbitrary predicate, list shape, or map shape does not generally prove that every possible value has been handled.

Composing structural patterns

Combine patterns with…To…
Sum typesSelect a case and unpack its payload
OptionalsExtract a value only when the expected shape is present
Error resultsMatch successful and failed outcomes after catch
JSON and other decoded dataReach a needed field through nested maps, lists, and unions
Tables and array viewsPreserve useful slice and column representations
Stream parsersClassify the structured records produced by a grammar

This fragment combines structural matching with the error system. It assumes load returns either a Config, FileNotFound, or PermissionDenied:

. label = match catch load(path)
    | config Config
        config.name
    | error FileNotFound
        "Use defaults"
    | error PermissionDenied
        "Ask for access"
  • Successful result: The typed capture recognizes and names the function's success value.
  • One error alternative: Prefix catch holds the error so a pattern can handle it as a value.
  • Another error alternative: The match keeps different recovery policies in one exhaustive decision.

The central composition rule is simple: an outer pattern establishes a shape, and each nested pattern receives the value at that position. Successful captures become ordinary typed names inside the selected result or branch.

Things to know

  • Arms are ordered. Put a specific pattern before another pattern that would also accept it.
  • _ matches without binding; ... changes the collection-length requirement.
  • A captured remainder may be a view of the original representation rather than a copied list.
  • Map patterns require the named keys but allow extra entries.
  • Structural text patterns match an existing complete string; stream patterns consume successive input.
  • Destructuring declares an expectation. Use match? or a conditional binding when failure is ordinary.
  • Exhaustiveness applies to closed alternatives, not every collection shape or predicate.

Continue with Sum types and enums for closed domain alternatives, Collections and data layout for the representations being matched, or Stream pattern matching for grammars over sequences.

Numerical units

Yumi can attach a unit to a number at the type level. A value such as 500ms is not a plain number followed by display text: it is a numeric value whose type is Milliseconds. Functions can name that type in their signatures, conversions can account for the relationship between milliseconds and seconds, and arithmetic can preserve the unit chosen by the expression.

Units are ordinary numeric classes. They inherit a machine representation from a numeric base such as F64 or I16, and they can participate in the rest of the class system. The unit suffix is a compact way to construct a value of one of those classes.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
16msA typed quantity, not a number with display text appended.
Unit equalityDeclare multiplicative relationships; conversions follow them transitively.
ArithmeticConvert the right operand to the left unit and preserve that unit.
AliasesUse short suffixes in literals and a canonical suffix for presentation.
LimitsNo automatic compound dimensions, cancellation, or offset conversions.

Unit literals

Write the unit immediately after an integer or floating-point literal:

  • Duration: The suffix chooses Milliseconds.
  • Angle: The suffix chooses Degrees.
  • Coordinate: A visible alias connects the literal to a numeric class.
  • Percentage: Supported symbol suffixes work too. There is no space before a suffix.
. frame-time = 16ms
. rotation = 90deg
. width = 200px
. opacity = 25%

The suffix determines the type of the entire literal. For example, 16ms has type Milliseconds and 90deg has type Degrees. In a type position, use the class name rather than its literal suffix:

+ frame-delay Milliseconds = 16ms

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ rotate
    - angle Degrees

Declaring a unit family

A unit family begins with a numeric class. Its first suffixed unit inherits from that family, and the remaining units state their size in terms of an existing unit:

  • Representation: The family uses floating-point storage and can own shared behavior.
  • Conversion equality: One microsecond equals one thousand nanoseconds. Chains compose transitively.
  • Literal aliases: Both spellings are accepted; the last, seconds, is the canonical suffix used by UnitString.
+ Duration is F64

+ Nanoseconds (ns) is Duration
+ Microseconds (µs) is 1000ns
+ Milliseconds (ms) is 1000µs
+ Seconds (s, seconds) is 1000ms
+ Minutes (minutes) is 60s
+ Hours (hours) is 60minutes

The family class is a useful home for behavior shared by every unit. In the standard library, Duration inherits from F64 and defines operations such as waiting, timers, and conversion to native time values. Every duration unit inherits that behavior through its base chain.

A unit does not need a separate family class when no shared domain is required. A direct numeric unit can be declared in one line:

+ Coord (px) is Float

Here, Coord is the type, px is its literal suffix, and Float supplies its representation and numeric behavior.

Converting values

Yumi converts between connected units when a surrounding type requires it:

. timeout Seconds = 1500ms
  • Destination type: The context requests seconds.
  • Source quantity: Implicit conversion stores 1.5seconds.

The value stored in timeout is 1.5seconds. Write an explicit cast when the destination is part of the expression rather than supplied by a declaration, argument, or return type:

. radians = 180° as Radians

Conversions use the product of the equalities connecting the source and destination. The direction of the conversion is derived automatically from the declaration, so declaring Seconds in terms of Milliseconds also permits conversion from seconds to milliseconds.

Unit equalities are multiplicative. They can express seconds and milliseconds, radians and degrees, or ratios and percentages. They cannot directly express conversions with an offset, such as two temperature scales with different zero points. Such conversions need functions or converters that perform the complete calculation.

Arithmetic and comparisons

For arithmetic between connected unit types, Yumi converts the right operand to the left operand's unit before applying the numeric operator. The result retains the left operand's unit.

ExpressionResult
8hours + 30minutes8.5hours
30minutes + 8hours510minutes
8hours - 30minutes7.5hours
180° as Radiansapproximately 3.141593rad

The same conversion makes comparisons between connected units natural. For example, 500ms < 1s compares the same quantity in a common unit.

The left-unit rule is significant: changing operand order can change the result type and its canonical presentation even when the quantities are equal. Choose the left operand deliberately when later code expects a particular unit.

Yumi's unit system is not dimensional analysis. Multiplication and division do not synthesize compound types such as meters per second, nor do they cancel matching units. Once connected operands have been converted, these operators perform ordinary numeric arithmetic and preserve the left unit. Programs that need types such as velocity, area, or energy should declare those domain types and the operations that produce them.

Connecting separately declared units

A public module-level equality can connect unit types that were declared independently:

+ 1csec = 1000000000cnsec
+ 1csec = 1seconds

This form is useful at system boundaries. In this example, native C time units are connected to each other and then to the Duration family. The conversion graph is transitive, so the second declaration also makes cnsec convertible to duration units through csec.

Both sides should be unit-bearing constants. A raw built-in numeric type does not identify a unit and is therefore not a suitable endpoint for an equality declaration.

Ratios and percentages

The standard units module defines normalized ratios and percentages with the same mechanism:

+ Ratio (%%) is F64
+ Percent (%) is 0.01%%
  • Normalized ratio: 1%% is one; 0.5%% is one half.
  • Percentage equality: 25% converts to 0.25%%, and 100% to 1%%.

The module also provides Scale and Scalable for mapping values to normalized ratios and between ranges. Scaling is built on numerical units, but it is separate from unit equality: a scale maps a position within a range, while a unit equality states that two numeric representations denote the same quantity.

Example: choosing an hour with a slider

The Hour type implements Scalable and advertises its range as Scale(0hour, 23hour). Therefore, 0.75%% as Hour produces 18hour. The cast maps the normalized ratio onto the range owned by Hour; the caller does not need to know or repeat its endpoints.

The leading zero is significant. 0.75%% is a ratio of three quarters, while 75%% is a ratio of seventy-five and would map far beyond the hour range. When starting with a percentage, `75% as Ratio produces the equivalent 0.75%%`.

Unit names and strings

Every numeric value exposes its canonical suffix through unit. Values without a unit return an empty suffix. Cast a value to UnitString when its unit should be included in its textual form:

. suffix = (2days).unit
. text = 2days as UnitString
  • Inspect the suffix: This returns "days".
  • Format with the unit: Use the underlying numeric formatting followed by the canonical suffix.

Standard unit families

The standard library uses numerical units in several domains:

  • /time/duration defines durations from nanoseconds through larger calendar approximations.
  • /math defines radians and degrees.
  • /units/distance defines a distance family.
  • /graphics/primitives uses px coordinates.
  • /tui/primitives uses tx terminal coordinates.
  • /units defines ratios, percentages, scales, and the Scalable interface.

These families all use the same language feature. Their differing behavior comes from the methods on their numeric classes and from the equalities declared between their units.

Designing units

  • Choose storage first. Use a floating-point base for fractional quantities. An integer-backed destination still has integer storage after conversion.
  • Keep equalities consistent. Prefer one obvious base and short conversion paths. Every path between the same types should agree.
  • Choose the last alias deliberately. It becomes the public suffix used by UnitString.
  • Stay within the model. Use explicit functions or domain types for offsets, compound dimensions, and relationships beyond a multiplicative ratio.

Collections and data layout

Yumi offers both everyday collections and more explicit control over how their data is stored. A list or map can express the application's data model. Arrays, views, bitmaps, and tables give the author more ways to match a representation to the operations performed on it.

These collections can also be stream sources. Choosing stored data does not prevent using the same sequence operations as a generator or a channel.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
List / map / rangeOrdered values, keyed values, or a compact progression.
Array / viewContiguous mutable storage, or access to a region of existing storage.
Immutable array / builderConstruct a collection, then expose fixed storage.
TablePresent rows while storing fields in separate columns.
BitmapRepresent positional Boolean choices as bits.
Backing storageChoose managed storage or a more explicit lifetime independently of layout.

Familiar collections

  • Ordered values: The list preserves the item order and type.
  • Keyed values: This map associates string keys with integers; its type shorthand is [String = Int].
  • Missing key: An absent lookup uses the fallback. The list type shorthand is [String].
. names = ["Ada", "Lin", "Sam"]
. scores = Map'String'Int()
scores["Ada"] = 10
scores["Lin"] = 12

-- ", ".join(names)
-- scores["Sam"] ?? 0

list += item and list.append(item) add exactly one item, even when that item is itself a collection. list ++= items and list.append-all(items) add each item of a stream in place. + and ++ are the copying counterparts.

Ranges describe a progression without spelling out every item. 1 .. 4 includes both endpoints; 0 .. < 4 excludes the upper endpoint. A range can supply loop bounds, stream input, or a slice specification.

Arrays make representation explicit

Array'Item, written Item[] in a type position, provides contiguous mutable array storage. Arrays are useful for indexed processing, binary data, native interfaces, and algorithms where layout matters.

. values = Array'Int([10, 20, 30, 40])
. middle = values[1 .. < 3]
-- ", ".join(middle)
  • Array storage: Choose contiguous mutable storage explicitly.
  • Region: The half-open slice selects 20, 30. A view stays connected to its backing storage rather than promising a separate snapshot.

That distinction matters when a function promises an independent snapshot. The source text of a slice does not, by itself, promise a deep copy. A small retained view may also keep a larger backing allocation reachable.

Construction and immutability

Yumi has immutable array storage and builder-oriented construction. This supports a common shape of algorithm: accumulate a result while constructing it, then expose a fixed collection for consumption.

An immutable collection limits mutation through that collection's interface. If its elements refer to mutable objects, those objects do not become deeply immutable merely because the container is immutable.

Backing storage is another dimension. Garbage-collected storage is convenient for ordinary application data. Arena-backed facilities make grouped lifetimes explicit. The choice can affect what may outlive a computation and which operations can allocate, so it belongs near the owner of the data rather than being scattered through unrelated consumers.

Tables separate rows from physical layout

A table can present rows while storing each field in its own column. This is a structure-of-arrays layout: all the x values together, all the y values together, and so on.

  • Construct rows: Describe three point-shaped values.
  • Read a column: Access the x coordinates together, producing 1, 2, 3.
  • Row shape: The type declares fields; the table stores each field in its own column.
/core/table

. points = Table'Point(3) • with Point(each + 1, each + 10)
-- ", ".join(points.x)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Point is Struct

+ x I32
+ y I32

Column layout can be useful when an operation reads one field across many rows. Processing every field of one row at a time has different access patterns. A table is therefore a representation choice, not a blanket promise that all operations become faster.

The distinction also makes some abstractions more interesting. Destructuring a supported table can expose columns; iterating it visits row-shaped values. The same underlying storage supports more than one useful view of the data.

Bitmaps represent compact choices

Bitmaps store Boolean information as bits. They are useful for flags, occupancy, selection, and other problems in which each position answers a yes-or-no question. Bitmap operations can count values, find positions, and search for runs without requiring a collection of separately represented Boolean elements.

This is another case where the representation expresses the problem. A set of selected rows may fit a bitmap more naturally than a list of objects. A map remains more appropriate when the question is about arbitrary keys rather than positions.

Stored data and streams work together

NeedUseful representation
Random access, reuse, or a stable stored resultCollection
Successive processing without retaining every itemStream
Transform stored itemsFeed a collection into a pipeline
Retain a finite pipeline's resultCollect it into a list or array

Structural patterns can inspect a collection's shape. Stream pipelines can transform its items. Neither requires the chapter using the collection to repeat its storage implementation.

The useful question is what must remain available, in what form, and for how long. Yumi gives that question answers ranging from a simple list literal to an explicitly owned region of columnar or native storage.

Streams

A stream is a source of values that a program can process in sequence. Those values might already be stored in a list, be calculated by a generator, or arrive through a connection. The consumer can use the same function in each case.

This is the central idea behind Yumi's streams: **describe the operation in terms of the values it consumes, without requiring a particular storage layout or delivery schedule.** Synchronous and asynchronous input do not need separate versions of that operation.

The abstraction connects several parts of the language. Loops consume streams. Generators, comprehensions, and stream pipelines produce them. Stream patterns recognize sequences and turn them into structured results. Channels connect producers to consumers, and reactive expressions expose changing values as streams. The standard library builds selection, aggregation, sorting, and combination on the same foundation.

At a glance

NeedYumi's model
Accept stored or arriving values<Item> accepts the whole stream family
Consume successive valuesfor, direct reads on readable sources, or a library consumer
Produce valuesGenerators, comprehensions, and pipelines
Recognize recordsStream patterns
Coordinate arrivalsTasks, channels, events, and reactive expressions
Know the costEstablish completion, replay, buffering, and ownership for the concrete source

One function, several kinds of stream

A parameter of type <Int> accepts the stream family for integers. This function reads at most three items and adds them. Its callers supply a list, a range, a generator, an immutable array, and a buffered broadcaster:

/core/array-builder

-- total-first-three([1, 2, 3, 100])
-- total-first-three(1 .. 10)
-- total-first-three(numbers())
-- total-first-three(ImmutableArray([1, 2, 3, 100]))

. published = AsyncBufferedChannel'Int()
