published <- 1
published <- 2
published <- 3
-- total-first-three(published)
published.close()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do total-first-three Int
    - values <Int>

. total = 0
. count = 0
for value in values
    total += value
    count += 1
    if count == 3
        break
= total

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do numbers

<= 1
<= 2
<= 3
<= 100
  • Stored inputs: A list and a range use the same call.
  • Published input: The buffered broadcaster retains these pre-subscription values.
  • One signature: Accept successive integers without requiring a list or immediate delivery.
  • Consumer boundary: Stop after three items; the broadcaster need not close first.
  • Generated input: Yielded values participate too. Every call prints 6.

Nothing in <Int> says that reading is immediate. A source may have to wait. The loop still has the same shape, and the function still has the same signature. Waiting affects when the answer is available, not how the consumer describes its calculation.

The stream family

<Item> is shorthand for Stream'Item. The core library defines Stream as an Or family of supported source types. Its declaration is:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Stream'T is CursorIterable'T || Indexable'T || Iterable'T || Broadcastable'T || ImmutableArray'T

Each alternative supplies items in its own way. A source may support more than one.

AlternativeHow it supplies itemsTypical use
CursorIterableSeparate iterator state, advanced by the sourceStrings, ranges, custom cursors
IndexableLength and indexed accessLists, mutable arrays, stored sequences
IterableOptional reads and iteration lifecycle hooksGenerators and synchronous channels
BroadcastableSubscription and publicationAsync channels and events
ImmutableArrayDirect access to immutable array storageFixed stored results

The compiler and adapters make operations work across this family without requiring one large common interface.

CursorIterable

CursorIterable'Item'State separates the source from the state of an iteration. The source provides an initial state and an operation that returns the next state together with an optional item. Absence indicates the end of that traversal.

This is useful when iteration has a natural cursor that need not be stored inside the source itself. A string, for example, can advance through its encoded characters using a position. Ranges also support cursor iteration. A new traversal can obtain a new initial state.

The state type need not be the item type. A source might yield characters while keeping a byte offset, or yield records while keeping several counters. The final section shows a complete implementation.

Indexable

Indexable'Item provides a length and indexed access. Lists, strings, ranges, and mutable arrays can participate through this interface.

An indexable source can be traversed without a consumable read cursor. It also makes operations such as accessing the first item possible without walking through the input. Being indexable does not, by itself, guarantee that indexing is constant-time or that the underlying values never change.

Some sources support more than one alternative. A range or string does not have to choose between being cursor-iterable and indexable; both capabilities can be useful to consumers.

Iterable

Iterable'Item is the read-based interface. It extends Readable'Item, whose <- operation returns an optional item. It also supplies iteration lifecycle hooks.

Generators and synchronous channels are examples. The next read may resume a producer, retrieve an already buffered value, or wait for another task. An iterable can carry progress inside itself, so do not assume that asking to iterate it again restarts the source.

The broad shorthand <Item> does not mean only Iterable'Item. Use the latter spelling when a function specifically needs the read-based interface rather than the entire family.

Broadcastable

Broadcastable'Item provides subscription and unsubscription. Values are delivered to subscribers instead of existing only for one reader to remove from a queue.

Async channels and event endpoints can supply this interface. Iteration can adapt a broadcaster into a readable sequence, but the source's publication and lifetime rules still matter. In particular, subscribing does not inherently mean receiving a replay of everything published earlier.

An event endpoint can expose Broadcastable'Item without exposing a writable channel. The right to observe a source and the right to publish into it are separate capabilities.

ImmutableArray

ImmutableArray'Item is explicitly included in the family. A consumer can work with immutable array storage directly, without requiring the author to wrap it in a generator first.

Immutability describes the array's storage interface. It does not mean that every object referenced by an item is deeply immutable.

What the common type does and does not promise

All five alternatives can supply items to stream operations. They do not all promise the same delivery behavior:

QuestionWhat to establish about the particular source
Can a read wait?Whether more values can arrive later
Can it be traversed again?Whether it can start a fresh traversal or has already advanced
Do two consumers see the same values?Independent traversal, competing reads, or broadcast delivery
Does it retain earlier values?Storage, buffering, or an explicit replay policy
How does it end?Exhaustion, generator completion, channel closure, or unsubscription
Can it be indexed?Whether it actually offers Indexable, not merely Stream

These questions describe the source. They are not reasons to duplicate a transformation into separate synchronous and asynchronous implementations.

Shorthand and signatures

Type notation

SpellingMeaning
<Int>Stream'Int
<Item>A stream family parameterized by Item
<<Int>>A stream whose items are themselves integer streams
[Int]List'Int, a stored list
Int[]Array'Int, contiguous mutable array storage
Int<>SyncChannel'Int

The position of the angle brackets matters. <Int> describes an accepted family of sources. Int<> describes a particular channel type. A parameter typed <Int> does not allocate a channel just because it is called a stream.

A generic transformation can preserve its source's item type while accepting different source implementations:

  • Infer the item type: The calls produce 1, 1, 2, 2 and a, a, b, b.
  • Preserve the relationship: The same declaration works for integers and characters.
  • Accept the family: The body needs successive items, not knowledge of the caller's storage.
-- List(twice([1, 2]))
-- List(twice("ab"))

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do twice'Item
    - values <Item>

for value in values
    <= value
    <= value

Use a narrower signature when it expresses a real requirement. An algorithm that must jump to arbitrary positions can ask for Indexable'Item. A component that installs subscriptions can ask for Broadcastable'Item. A function that only needs a sequence should usually accept <Item> and leave the representation to its caller.

Expression notation

Angle brackets around an expression mean something different. <#count * 2> creates a reactive stream of the expression's values, with #count marking a tracked dependency. It is not a cast to the stream type and not another spelling of a one-element list.

The type and expression forms meet naturally: a reactive expression produces a source that can be passed to a stream-oriented function. The details of tracked reads appear in Concurrency and reactivity.

Consuming values

Iteration

for value in source processes successive items. The source determines how the next item becomes available. The loop ends when the source is exhausted, or when the body exits early.

Loop clauses can filter or bound a traversal. This example skips values that do not satisfy when:

for value in 1 .. 6 when value % 2 == 0
    -- value
  • Input: Visit an inclusive range.
  • Filter: Only even values reach the body, printing 2, 4, and 6.

It prints 2, 4, and 6 on separate lines. while and until clauses can end a traversal according to a condition. An explicit break is useful when the stopping decision belongs inside the body.

Reading one item

For a readable source, <- source obtains one optional item. This generator supplies two values and then completes:

. source = numbers()
-- <- source
-- <- source
-- (<- source) ?? -1

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do numbers

<= 10
<= 20
  • Read an item: The first two reads produce 10 and 20.
  • Observe completion: The generator's final read is absent, so the fallback produces -1. Zero or false would still be present items.

For a waiting channel, temporary lack of input is different from completion: the read can suspend until a sender provides an item or the channel closes. Not every Readable has identical waiting behavior, however. Use the concrete source's contract rather than treating every absent direct read as proof that no future publication is possible.

Collecting and joining

Materialization means consuming values and storing the resulting collection:

. source = 1 .. 4
. values = List(source)
-- values
-- ", ".join(values)
  • Collect: Consume the finite source into reusable storage.
  • Make text: Consume stored values to produce 1, 2, 3, 4.

Collecting is a policy decision. It uses memory for the result, waits for the input to finish, and turns a traversal into reusable stored data. An unbounded or never-closed source cannot be collected to completion. Restrict such a source before applying a consumer that needs its end.

Waiting does not change the function

Here the same total function works on a list and a channel fed by another task:

  • Separate producer: Create another task explicitly; the consumer loop is not implicitly parallel.
  • End the sequence: total needs to know when no more values will arrive.
  • Ordinary call: The channel call may wait; both calls print 6, without await.
  • Ordinary function: The same helper accepts the list and the channel, without an async declaration.
-- total([1, 2, 3])

. incoming Int<>
do new
    incoming <- 1
    incoming <- 2
    incoming <- 3
    incoming.close()

-- total(incoming)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do total Int
    - values <Int>

. result = 0
for value in values
    result += value
= result

Producing values

Generator functions

A generator uses <= to supply one item and <<= to supply the items from another source:

  • Yield one: Supply an individual item.
  • Yield a source: Supply all items from another source. The complete output is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
-- List(sequence())

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do sequence

<= 1
<<= 2 .. 4
<= 5

An absent optional value can be omitted with <=?. Completion means that there are no more items to yield. A stored generator represents an ongoing traversal; call its producing function again when you need a fresh instance rather than assuming the old one rewinds.

Comprehensions

A comprehension describes an output expression over an input source:

. squares = each * each in 1 .. 5 when each % 2 != 0
-- List(squares)
  • Output expression: Square each participating input.
  • Source: Visit the inclusive range.
  • Selection: Only odd values participate, producing 1, 9, 25.

Use a generator when producing the sequence needs a more substantial procedure. Use a stream pipeline when the sequence is best described as contributions followed by several stages. These forms can feed one another and the same consumers.

Stream pipelines

Stream pipelines assemble and transform sequences. A source can contribute individual items or expand another stream, then filter, map, or observe the values that pass through it. Stages run as their output is consumed; the source itself may already be active independently.

The Stream pipelines chapter covers the construction markers, each, optional contributions, stage ordering, and the library operations for aggregation, selection, combination, and buffering. Those operations work with the source family described here.

Stream pattern matching

A stream can also be the input to a grammar. A pattern can recognize a record, capture pieces of it, and return a structured value. The same grammar can work over stored text or characters arriving through a channel, without a separate asynchronous parser.

Stream pattern matching covers named rules, captures, repetition, lookahead, and parsing non-text items. It also explains a significant distinction: matching a whole input may need to wait for its end, while recognizing successive records can continue on a connection that stays open.

Concurrency and reactivity

Channels and reactive expressions are sources in the same stream family. A loop can consume their values without prescribing how a producer is scheduled. A publication can also feed subscribers, and a latest-value expression can make changing state available to another calculation.

Concurrency and reactivity explains tasks, channel delivery models, events, subscriptions, tracked reads, and latest values. That chapter also covers the closure and ownership rules that distinguish a queue from a broadcaster.

Completion, errors, and cleanup

  • Errors can arrive during consumption. Catching a factory call alone does not cover later reads; recovery belongs around the work that pulls values.
  • Traversal has a lifecycle. Iterable supplies begin-iterating and end-iterating; the broadcaster adapter uses them to subscribe and unsubscribe.
  • Cleanup has an owner. A generator can register do finally. Ending its traversal does not automatically destroy a caller-owned socket or stop an independent producer.

See Errors for propagation, recovery, and cleanup syntax, and Concurrency and reactivity for channel closure. For every source, ask what ends this traversal and who owns the producer.

Replay, storage, and cost

A stream is not a promise of replay

Keep these cases separate:

  • A list can be traversed again because its items are stored.
  • A cursor source can start another traversal from a new initial state.
  • A generator instance retains its current progress.
  • A channel read can remove an item that another reader will no longer see.
  • A broadcaster can publish values that late subscribers never receive.

Calling a generator-producing function again can create a new traversal. Retaining and reusing the already-created generator is a different operation. Likewise, materializing a source once and iterating the resulting list differs from re-running the producer twice. The latter may repeat IO or see changed state.

Incremental does not mean constant memory

A plain map or filter can often pass one item at a time. Other operations retain information:

Operation or sourcePossible retained state
scanThe accumulator, whose own size may grow
distinctPreviously seen values or keys
pairwiseThe preceding item
Grouping buffersItems awaiting a complete group
Sorting or reversalThe complete finite input
Replaying a one-pass inputA materialized sequence
Queued channelsItems not yet consumed
Pattern lookahead and backtrackingInput needed to retry or complete recognition

The source can also retain storage independently of the pipeline. Holding a small result may keep an owner alive, and an abandoned consumer can leave an independent producer active. Consider the entire producer-adapter-consumer lifetime when investigating retained memory.

Compilation can remove intermediate machinery

The compiler can fuse eligible producers and consumers, so a chain of stream operations does not necessarily allocate one iterator object or call one callback for every stage. An escaping, independently resumable generator can still need its own state.

These optimizations do not change the intended sequence of effects, error propagation, or cleanup. They also do not make sorting incremental or erase buffering required by the algorithm. Treat performance as something to measure for the actual source and consumer, rather than as a property guaranteed by the word “stream.”

Implementing a source

The simplest producer is usually a generator. Implement a protocol directly when the source has a representation or lifecycle that deserves one.

A cursor source provides the initial state and a next-state operation. This source yields 2, 5, and 8:

-- List(Steps(3))

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Steps is Tuple
    is CursorIterable'Int'Int

+ limit Int

────────────────────
+ get initial-iterator-state Int

0

────────────────────
+ do next-iterator (Int, Int?)
    - state Int

. absent Int?
if state >= limit
    = (state, absent)
= (state + 1, 2 + state * 3)
  • Item and state types: Both are integers here, but their roles are separate.
  • Fresh traversal: Start with state zero.
  • Completion: An absent item reports exhaustion.
  • Advance and yield: Return the new cursor and the current item. List collects 2, 5, 8 without special knowledge of Steps.

For a read-based source, implement the Iterable contract, including the optional read and the iteration lifecycle hooks. For random access, implement Indexable. For publications, implement Broadcastable with clear subscription, closure, and delivery behavior. A bare Readable is useful for direct reads but is not, by itself, one of the Stream alternatives.

The goal is not to make every source look like the same object internally. It is to make the operations that only need a sequence reusable across sources. Storage, waiting, parsing, and delivery can then vary while the function expressing the actual calculation stays the same.

Stream pipelines

A stream pipeline describes a sequence of values, one contribution per line. Some lines contribute a single value, some contribute an existing sequence, and some contribute only when a value is present. Together, they let the shape of the code follow the shape of the result.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Construct* contributes an item; ** expands a source; add ? to omit absent contributions.
Transform?> filters, *> maps, and ?*> maps present results.
Observe*\|> performs an effect and forwards the same item.
ConsumeA loop, List, join, or another consumer determines when stages run.
Combine and summarizeLibrary operations add reduction, selection, combination, buffering, and sorting.

Contributions become a stream

  • Consumer: Collect the resulting stream into a stored list.
  • One item: * contributes one value.
  • Expand a source: ** contributes every item from this inclusive range. The full result is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
-- List
    * 1
    ** 2 .. 4
    * 5

Building a sequence

Use * when the expression to its right is one item in the result. Use ** when that expression contains items to include individually.

This distinction matters for collections. * [2, 3] contributes a list as one item; ** [2, 3] contributes the numbers 2 and 3. An expansion marker expands its immediate operand; it does not recursively flatten everything inside it.

For a short, fixed list, [1, 2, 3] is usually enough. Stream pipelines become useful when a sequence mixes fixed items, optional items, and values drawn from elsewhere.

. include-debug = true
. extras = ["timing", "memory"]
-- List
    * "status"
    *? "debug" if include-debug
    ** extras
    * "done"
  • Fixed entry: Always include the status item.
  • Conditional entry: Omit debug when the condition is false.
  • Additional entries: Expand the list in place. The result is status, debug, timing, memory, done.

Optional contributions

Adding ? to a construction marker makes its operand optional:

FormContribution
* valueOne item
** valuesEvery item from a sequence
*? optional-valueOne item if the value is present
**? optional-valuesEvery item from a sequence if the sequence is present

An expression such as "debug" if include-debug produces an optional value. *? includes its present value or contributes nothing when it is absent. It does not insert an empty placeholder.

**? applies the same choice to a whole sequence:

. extras = [2, 3] if false
-- List
    * 1
    **? extras
    * 4
  • Optional expansion: An absent sequence contributes nothing. The result is 1, 4; with a true condition it would be 1, 2, 3, 4.

Transforming the stream

Once a stream has been described, subsequent stages can filter or transform its items. Inside each stage, each names the item arriving at that stage.

  • Input: Begin with six integers.
  • Filter: Keep even values.
  • Map: Multiply each retained value by ten, producing 20, 40, 60. Here each is the filter's output.
-- List
    ** 1 .. 6
    ?> each % 2 == 0
    *> each * 10

Read these stages from top to bottom. Every stage receives the output of the preceding stage, so changing their order can change the result. After a map, each refers to the mapped value.

StageMeaning
*> expressionProduce the expression's result for each input item
?> conditionKeep the input item when the condition is true
?*> optional-expressionProduce each present result and omit absent results
*\|> effectEvaluate the effect and pass the input item through unchanged

?*> combines transformation with omission:

-- List
    ** 1 .. 6
    ?*> each * 10 if each % 2 == 0
  • Map present results: Emit the transformed value when present; omit absence. This also produces 20, 40, 60.

Stage bodies are expressions

A stage evaluates the expression written after its operator for each item that reaches it. To call a function, write the call explicitly:

-- List
    ** 1 .. 3
    *> double(each)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ double Int
    - value Int

value * 2
  • Call explicitly: The expression invokes double for every item, producing 2, 4, 6.
Stage expressionWhat it produces
*> double(each)The result of calling double
*> doubleThe function value itself
*> 7A 7 for each input
*> make()A fresh call result for each input, even without mentioning each

Stages can also follow an existing stream directly. These fragments assume values is a stream and double is a function:

values ?> each > 0
values *> double(each)

There is no need to wrap an existing stream in another construction block just to transform it.

When the work happens

Pipeline stages are lazy: constructing the pipeline does not evaluate their bodies. A consumer pulls items through the stages as it needs them. List requests all the items to build a stored collection; a loop can stop early.

The tap stage, *|>, makes this timing visible. It performs an effect for each item reaching it, then forwards that same item:

  • Tap: Record an item only when consumption brings it through this stage.
  • Pull: Creating the pipeline does not run the tap; iteration does.
  • Stop early: The third item never reaches the tap.
. values =
    ** 1 .. 3
    *|> record(each)
-- "created"
for value in values
    -- "out $value"
    if value == 2
        break

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do record
    - value Int

-- "tap $value"

The output is:

created
tap 1
out 1
tap 2
out 2

Nothing is recorded when values is assigned. The loop pulls two items, then stops, so the tap never sees 3. An unconsumed pipeline does not run its tap, even if the pipeline appears as a standalone expression.

A tap runs when an item reaches that stage. A later filter may still discard the item. Place the tap after the filter when the effect should apply only to items the filter keeps. For immediate iteration whose purpose is an effect, an explicit for loop makes that intent clear.

Choosing stream pipelines

Stream pipelines are useful when the result is naturally described as contributions followed by transformations: a menu with optional entries, a sequence assembled from several sources, or a filtered stream of names to join into text. Start with what belongs in the result, then put the stages that refine it underneath.

Keep the consumer visible when timing matters. The same stream pipeline can feed a stored list or a stream consumed a little at a time, and that choice determines when its stages do their work.

Standard-library operations

Stream syntax and library operations work together. The /stream module re-exports the main operation groups; importing a specific module such as /stream/aggregate keeps an example's dependencies focused.

Function names alone are not enough to determine whether an operation consumes the input, produces another stream, or stores intermediate values. The examples below show the current library's behavior, including a few names whose meanings may differ from other libraries.

Aggregation and running results

/stream/aggregate

-- sum([1, 2, 3])
-- reduce(10, [1, 2, 3]) • using :: total, item => total + item
-- List(scan(0, [1, 2, 3]) • using :: total, item => total + item)
-- first(List'Int()) ?? -1
-- some([1, 2, 3]) • where each == 2
  • Final accumulator: Start at 10 and produce 16 after consuming the input.
  • Running results: Yield 1, 3, 6; the seed is not an extra emitted item.
  • Empty input: An absent first item falls back to -1.

The output is:

6
16
1, 3, 6
-1
true

reduce computes one final accumulator. scan exposes its intermediate values as a stream; the seeded form emits the updated accumulator for each input, rather than emitting the seed as an extra first item.

OperationConsumption and result
count, sum, reduceConsume the input to produce a final answer
scan, scan-mapProduce incremental accumulator results
firstSelect the first item; empty input is absent
lastConsume to the end; empty input is absent
headtailSplit the first item from the remaining source
someStop once a predicate succeeds
all from /stream/aggregateStop once a predicate fails; true for empty input
min, max, averageSummarize the complete input

Empty-input policies differ. Unseeded reduce currently returns the item type's default value for an empty source; the seeded form returns its seed. min and max use the unseeded reduction behavior. Do not infer an optional result or an exception just from familiarity with another language's API. Use a seed or an explicit empty check when the distinction belongs in the domain model.

The inspection module also exposes stream-producing predicates. For example, contains(1, values) from /stream/inspect returns a stream carrying a Boolean. That is different from the direct Boolean returned by some in /stream/aggregate.

Selection and repetition

/stream/combine
/stream/filter

-- List(take(2, [10, 20, 30, 40]))
-- List(repeat(2, [3, 4]))
-- List(distinct([1, 1, 2, 1]))
-- List(distinct-until-changed([1, 1, 2, 1]))
  • Select a position: This library's take(2) yields 30, the item at zero-based position two.
  • Remember seen values: Yield 1, 2 across the traversal.
  • Compare adjacent keys: Yield 1, 2, 1; a value may return after a different one.

This prints:

30
3, 4, 3, 4
1, 2
1, 2, 1

In the current library, take(n) selects the item at zero-based position n and yields that item. It does not mean “take the first n items.” take-last(n) selects by the corresponding distance from the end and must reach the end first. Use bounded iteration when you mean a prefix of the source. Other take overloads stop according to a terminator stream or pair items with an interval stream.

distinct remembers earlier keys or values across the traversal. Its memory can grow with the number of distinct items. distinct-until-changed compares against the preceding retained key and allows a value to appear again after a different value. Key-selector overloads let the program state which part of an item determines equality.

repeat repeats a source's sequence. Replayable inputs can be traversed again; a one-pass iterable may need to be collected so subsequent repetitions have something to read. A mutable source traversed again can expose mutations made between traversals.

Combining sources

/stream/combine

-- List(zip([1, 2, 3], [10, 20]) *> (each[0] + each[1]))
-- List(product([1, 2], [3, 4]) *> (each[0] * 10 + each[1]))
-- List(flat-map([[1, 2], [3, 4]]))
  • Corresponding items: Form pairs until one input ends.
  • Every combination: Pair each first-source item with each second-source item.
  • Inner sequences: Consume the inner streams, yielding 1, 2, 3, 4.

This prints 11, 22, then 13, 14, 23, 24, then 1, 2, 3, 4.

OperationRelationship between inputs
andConsume the first source, then the second
orMerge inputs through concurrently running producers
zipPair corresponding items; stop when a pair can no longer be formed
productPair each item of the first source with each item of the second
flat-mapConsume the inner streams of a stream of streams
indexedAttach a zero-based index to each item

Concatenation and merging answer different questions. Concatenation preserves the complete first sequence before beginning the second; if the first never ends, the second is never reached. Merging allows arrivals from either producer and does not promise one global order independent of scheduling.

zip can wait for the slower side. product needs to revisit the second source, and its iterable overload materializes that input for reuse. The mathematical result is the same across source families, but the storage and lifetime consequences can differ.

Buffering, adjacent items, and sorting

/stream/coincidence
/stream/sort

-- " | ".join(buffer(2, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))
-- " | ".join(pairwise([1, 2, 3]))
-- sort([3, 1, 2])
  • Complete groups: Emit 1, 2 and 3, 4; the incomplete final group is omitted.
  • Adjacent pairs: Retain one previous item, producing (1, 2) and (2, 3).
  • Stored ordering: Consume the finite input before producing sorted values.

This prints 1, 2 | 3, 4, then (1, 2) | (2, 3), then 1, 2, 3.

The count-based buffer emits complete groups. In the current implementation, an incomplete final group is not emitted. Its no-count overload has a different purpose: it starts a producer task and returns a buffered stream. These two meanings should not be confused.

pairwise retains the preceding item and emits adjacent pairs. partition routes values into two buffered outputs according to a predicate. Consumers that neglect one output can allow its retained values to grow.

The current window operation is also worth reading by its actual contract: its predicate form retains the first item, matching items, and a final nonmatching item when present. It is not a generic fixed-width sliding-window API.

sort and reversed need stored input. They are natural operations on finite sources and poor fits for an unbounded source unless the program first defines a finite group to order.

See Streams for the common source family, and Batteries included for the wider library tour.

Stream pattern matching

Stream patterns recognize sequences of items. This differs from a structure pattern that inspects the fields or case of one value. A stream pattern can consume a word, a line, a packet, or a sequence of typed events and produce a value describing what it recognized.

The pattern machinery works with the stream's input type. Character patterns are convenient for text, but streams of bytes and objects are also meaningful inputs.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Sequence recognitionMatch successive characters, bytes, or objects with ~.
Captures and transformationsTurn recognized input into text, tuples, or domain values.
Named rulesBuild reusable grammars from pattern functions and local rules.
Whole input / record streamValidate a complete input or recognize successive records.
Stored / arriving inputUse one grammar; reads can wait without a separate async parser.
CostLookahead and backtracking may buffer input; effects do not automatically roll back.

Matching text and extracting a result

  • Sequence pattern: ~ begins recognition with a literal prefix.
  • Capture: Bind one or more lowercase characters as value.
  • Boundary and result: Require a newline, then return the captured name. This prints ada.
. name = match "name:ada\n"
    ~ "name:" value [a-z]+ "\n"
        value
    ?? "invalid"
-- name

The transformation can construct a tuple, a domain object, or another value; it need not return the original text. This is how recognition and parsing fit into ordinary expressions.

Pattern vocabulary

The following are pattern fragments, rather than standalone Yumi programs:

PatternMeaning
"name:"Match literal text
[a-z]Match a character in the indicated range
.Match one input item
a bMatch a followed by b
a \| bTry alternatives in order
(pattern)Group a pattern
pattern?Match an optional occurrence
pattern*Match zero or more occurrences
pattern+Match one or more occurrences
pattern{3}Match a specified number of occurrences
name patternCapture the pattern's result
\wordInvoke a named rule
&patternPositive lookahead: require a match without consuming it
!patternNegative lookahead: require a failure without consuming input

Choice is ordered. Place the alternatives deliberately, especially when one can match a prefix of another. Lookahead lets a rule check context before committing its consuming part. A repetition must be able to make progress; a rule that succeeds without consuming input is not a useful body for an unbounded repetition.

Named rules and structured results

A pattern function declares its input item type with ~ Char. Another pattern calls it with a backslash:

  • Invoke a rule: A backslash calls a named pattern.
  • Pattern function: Declare character input and a string result; no do is used.
  • Local rule: Name a reusable piece of the grammar. The outer rule exposes the name and prints ada.
-- match "name:ada\n"
    ~ \name-record
    ?? "invalid"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ name-record ~ Char String

~ "name:" name \word "\n"
    name

.. word String ~
    ~ [a-z]+

Rules can take arguments, refer to other rules, and recurse. A grammar is therefore written as Yumi declarations, with ordinary values available to its transformations. Pattern functions do not use do on their declarations.

Optional and repeated captures carry the corresponding absence or repetition in their result shape. Repetition over a character pattern can capture text; repetition over a rule that produces a domain value can collect those transformed values. Do not assume that every capture is a string just because the input is text.

Failure is a choice at the boundary

A failed match can produce absence, select a ?? fallback, or return an explicit error. This parser treats malformed input as a recoverable InvalidRecord:

-- parse-name("name:ada\n")
-- catch parse-name("invalid\n")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ InvalidRecord is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ parse-name String ?! InvalidRecord
    - source <Char>

match source
    ~ "name:" name [a-z]+ "\n"
        name
    ?! InvalidRecord("Expected a name record")
  • Source family: Accept any supported character stream.
  • Successful recognition: Produce the name.
  • Boundary policy: Treat malformed input as a recoverable error. The calls print ada and Expected a name record.

Whole input versus successive records

A root stream match checks the whole input. For example, matching "foo." against just "foo" does not accept the trailing period. This is useful for validating a complete document, but a connection that stays open after a record has not reached end of input.

For successive records, a pattern comprehension can recognize one record at a time:

  • Successive records: Recognize a record at a time and produce a stream of results.
  • Consume results: Join the names into ada, bob.
. source = "name:ada\nname:bob\n"
-- ", ".join(~ \name-record in source)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ name-record ~ Char String

~ "name:" name [a-z]+ "\n"
    name

This prints ada, bob. The result is itself a stream and can feed a pipeline or another consumer. A pipe can run every record under one helper, evaluated once as the pipe starts to read: source ~> \name-record with helper. Pattern iteration is not a promise to skip arbitrary invalid text: decide how unrecognized input should terminate or report failure, and express that policy in the parser.

The same parser with arriving input

The function below accepts <Char>. It first receives a stored string, then a channel whose characters are sent by another task:

-- parse-name("name:ada\n")

. incoming Char<>
do new
    for char in "name:bob\n"
        incoming <- char
    incoming.close()

-- parse-name(incoming)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ InvalidRecord is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ parse-name String ?! InvalidRecord
    - source <Char>

match source
    ~ "name:" name [a-z]+ "\n"
        name
    ?! InvalidRecord("Expected a name record")
  • Arriving characters: Another task supplies input one character at a time.
  • Whole-input boundary: Close the channel so the root match can establish end of input.
  • Same parser: The grammar, result type, and call spelling stay the same. The calls print ada and bob.

Networking uses the same principle. Given /net/socket and a peer that sends a sequence of these records, the following fragment adapts its character input and consumes parsed names:

  • Owned lifetime: Register closure for the socket acquired here.
  • Readable characters: Adapt transport input to the grammar's stream model.
  • Record boundary: Process names without requiring the peer to close after each record.
. socket = TCP'Char(host, port)
do finally
    socket.close()
. characters = socket as Iterable'Char
for name in ~ \name-record in characters
    -- name

host, port, and name-record are supplied by the surrounding program. The fragment has no async declaration or await, and it does not require the peer to close after every record. Connection setup, transport errors, and the lifetime of the socket still need the application's policy.

Matching non-text items

A pattern can recognize a sequence of typed objects too:

. events Event<>
do new
    events <- Click()
    events <- Click()
    events <- Key()
    events.close()

-- match events
    ~ clicks Click* key Key
        clicks.length
    ?? 0

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Event

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Click is Event

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Key is Event
  • Object pattern: Recognize zero or more clicks followed by a key event.
  • Transformed result: Count the captured clicks. The example prints 2.

Byte-oriented patterns can also decode typed fields and use a preceding length to control a later repetition. This is useful for packet formats, but byte order, decoding, and framing belong in the format's explicit contract.

Buffering, lookahead, and backtracking

The matcher needs a logical cursor that it can restore while trying alternatives. An already-stored source and a source that must be read from a socket provide that ability in different ways. Token-stream adapters can retain input so a failed alternative can rewind without asking an external producer to send the data again.

MechanismConsequence
BacktrackingRevisit buffered input; do not reverse network IO
Long speculationPotentially retain substantial input
Record pipeline (~>)Release input once its record is delivered; retain only the unfinished record
Input that arrives in piecesContinue from the item where the input ran out; never match the record again from its start, so each action runs once
Iterable or generator sourcePull one item at a time, so a complete record is delivered without waiting for more
Whole-input matchWait for completion even after recognizing a plausible prefix
LookaheadPossibly request more input to establish the condition

Avoid treating arbitrary side effects inside speculative parsing as automatically reversible. Yumi has explicit facilities for helper state and rollback, but cursor rewind alone is not a transaction over the application. Prefer constructing a result and applying effects after accepting it. Detailed custom materialization and rollback protocols warrant a separate grammar reference.

Where this fits

Stream patterns describe recognition over successive input items. Structural patterns inspect the shape of an existing value; stream pipelines describe how to produce or transform a sequence. These features compose: a grammar can yield records that a pipeline filters and a structural match classifies. See Streams for the source types that make the same parser useful over stored and arriving input.

Concurrency and reactivity

Yumi can wait for IO, coordinate independent tasks, publish events, and keep expressions connected to changing state. These are related capabilities, but each answers a different question: when work can proceed, who receives a value, or what should update after a change.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
WaitingOrdinary calls can suspend; no async/await calling convention.
Tasksdo new explicitly starts independent scheduled work.
DeliveryChoose rendezvous, queues, or subscriptions according to who should receive each item.
Reactive expressions<#value> produces updates; ##source reads a latest value.
OwnershipClosing, cancellation, and subscription lifetime remain explicit design choices.

Waiting without changing the call syntax

A function can call a network operation that suspends the current task while waiting for IO. Its callers do not need a different spelling just because that wait occurs somewhere below them. This fragment assumes a URL named url and imports from /net/http:

  • Caller: Invoke the helper normally and print its answer.
  • Helper: No async declaration is needed.
  • Network request: This call can suspend for IO. Neither this call nor its caller needs await.
-- page-body(url)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ page-body String
    - url URL

page.text

.. page = http-get(url)

This makes it easier to introduce a helper or replace a local source with a remote one. The operation still has a timing contract: a call can take time, fail, or allow other tasks to make progress before it returns. State observed before an IO call may need to be reconsidered afterward. The absence of a marker does not imply uninterrupted execution.

Tasks make concurrent work explicit

do new starts work in another task. Channels let the tasks exchange values:

  • Rendezvous channel: Connect producer and consumer.
  • Create work: Start the producer in another task.
  • Complete the source: The consumer can finish after reading 42.
. results Int<>
do new
    results <- 21 * 2
    results.close()

for value in results
    -- value

Yumi tasks are lightweight scheduled work, often called green threads. Native workers provide another level of execution, and the language includes parallel task forms. A program can overlap operations that spend time waiting or place work on native threads when it needs parallel execution.

Those are separate decisions. Starting a task does not promise one new operating-system thread per operation, and a loop over a stream does not implicitly parallelize its body. The source of a value, its delivery mechanism, and the placement of the work can be chosen independently.

Shared state and lifetimes

Channels give concurrent code a way to communicate values explicitly. Mutexes and other synchronization facilities are available when tasks or threads coordinate shared state. Task-local and thread-local declarations distinguish state associated with one task from state associated with its executing native thread.

A mutex held across an operation that can wait has different consequences from one held around a short update. Moving work to another thread also raises questions that cooperative task scheduling alone does not settle. Clear ownership is useful in both cases: who may change the state, and what event makes that change visible to another participant?

Tasks can also be canceled. Cancellation, normal completion, and a consumer losing interest are related but distinct events. A producer should have a way to finish and release resources, and a consumer should not assume that dropping its own result automatically ends every independent task behind it.

State transitions

Yumi includes state-machine constructs for behavior organized around named states and transitions. This is useful when the question is what an object may do next: a connection can be opening, active, or closing; a component can wait for input before continuing an action.

An explicit state model keeps those transitions together. Events and tasks can trigger progress while the machine describes which transitions belong to the current state. State machines covers the declarations, payloads, nested states, and subscription lifetimes, including how event transitions run to completion before a publication returns.

Channels and subscriptions

A channel makes the connection between a producer and consumer explicit. Writing an item uses destination <- value; a readable channel can supply an item through <- source. destination <-* source writes a source's items to the destination.

The core library provides several delivery models:

TypeMain behavior
SyncChannel'ItemRendezvous between a writer and reader; operations can wait for their counterpart
SyncBufferedChannel'ItemQueue items for readers; an empty open channel can wait for input
AsyncChannel'ItemPublish to current subscribers without retaining a pre-subscription history
AsyncBufferedChannel'ItemBuffer publications while there are no subscribers, then deliver buffered values on subscription
AsyncOnDemandChannel'Item'UsedAssociate active subscriptions with acquisition and release of an underlying resource

The names do not divide the stream world into “can suspend” and “cannot suspend.” A SyncChannel can suspend the current task while waiting. A Broadcastable can invoke subscribers synchronously. Delivery, buffering, and task scheduling are separate questions.

Buffered also does not imply bounded. If producers outrun consumers, queued data can grow. A rendezvous channel directly couples producer progress to consumer readiness; buffering relaxes that coupling by spending memory.

Iteration versus subscription

for item in source consumes a traversal. for item on source installs a subscription. The latter lets subsequent code continue while the handler remains interested in arrivals. The lifetime and ownership of that subscription matter.

This example uses a declared event, whose publication delivers to its subscribers synchronously:

  • Subscribe: Install a handler, then continue with subsequent code.
  • Publication: This event delivers during the publishing call: before, heard 42, after.
  • Declared event: Expose a stream source for subscribers.
. source = Source()
for value on source.changed
    -- "heard $value"

-- "before"
source.emit(42)
-- "after"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Source

+ event changed Int

────────────────────
+ do emit
    - value Int

changed <- value

Multiple subscribers can each observe a publication. Multiple readers of a queue instead take items from that queue; they do not automatically each receive a copy. A subscription can stop with break from its handler, and low-level subscribers can explicitly unsubscribe. Class-owned subscriptions and event endpoints also have owner lifetimes.

Closing is part of the protocol

Close a finite channel when the producer finishes; otherwise a consumer may wait indefinitely.

Closing delivers first, then ends. Every item a channel accepted before close() still reaches the readers or subscribers it was headed for, even when the close comes in the same turn as the write. After that, readers see the end of the stream and subscriptions end. A write after closing does what it did before: SyncChannel and AsyncChannel panic, and the other channels drop the item.

SourceAfter closing
SyncChannelA writer still waiting hands its item to the next reader; then reads end
SyncBufferedChannelReads drain the queued items, then end
AsyncChannelEach subscription gets the items queued for it, then ends
AsyncBufferedChannelSubscriptions get their queued items; reads drain the buffer kept for future subscribers; no new subscriptions
AsyncOnDemandChannelSubscriptions get their queued items; the underlying resource is released at the close

Stopping a subscription is different from closing its channel. A subscription that stops, by break or a while or until clause, by its owner going away, or by an explicit unsubscribe, drops any items still queued for it. That holds even while its closed channel is still delivering to other subscribers.

Stopping a consumer does not automatically stop every independent producer task or close a socket owned elsewhere. If a producer might otherwise keep working or block on a write, give the consumer and producer an explicit completion or cancellation arrangement.

Reactive streams and latest values

Streams can represent changes to an expression, not only explicit sends or generator yields. The expression form <expression> creates a stream, and tracked reads identify the state whose changes should cause new values to be produced:

  • Tracked expression: #count identifies the dependency; the initial value is 20.
  • Update: Changing the binding produces the next value, 30.
  • Lifetime: Finish observing when the consumer no longer needs updates.
.. count = 2
. values = <#count * 10>
-- <- values
count = 3
-- <- values
values.close()

Tracked property reads use forms such as model.#count. Tracking applies to supported state locations; it is not a promise that any arbitrary getter can be observed automatically.

The ## form goes in the other direction: it makes a stream's latest value available to a surrounding expression. A fragment such as .. current = ##updates gives a name to that latest-value expression. Inside a live declaration, stream arrivals can cause dependent expressions to be re-evaluated.

RequirementModel
Process each log record or transactionConsume every item
Show the current state when a display updatesRead the latest value
Retain a history or compute an aggregateStore or reduce the stream explicitly

A latest-value read does not guarantee that rendering observes every intermediate value.

Reactive streams have subscription lifetimes too. Arrange an owner or explicit cleanup for them, especially when the source outlives the display or computation observing it. Detailed markup and stylesheet behavior belongs in the corresponding UI documentation; the stream model supplies their sequence of updates.

State machines

A state machine describes what can happen next. A connection can be waiting, connected, or closing; a form can be editing, submitting, or showing a result. Yumi gives those states, their transitions, and the work that belongs to each state a place in the language.

The same declaration can carry data into a state, listen for events while it is active, and release its subscriptions when it exits. This keeps the lifetime of an operation close to the conditions under which the program should care about it.

At a glance

CapabilityFormWhat it gives you
Name a machine+ phase ~>A declaration whose body is its cases, like a function body.
Declare a state~> waitingA named case; the first untriggered case is the initial state.
React to an event~> ready on sourceEnter a case when the source emits.
Continue from a statethen ready on sourceA transition available while the enclosing state is active.
Capture event datafor pattern on sourceMatch the event and bind values for the target state.
Filter an eventon source when conditionCheck a guard for each arrival.
Decide on entryif conditionChoose an immediate transition when the owning scope enters.
Run state-owned workdo, do finallyActions on entry and exit.
Handle events while activefor value on source in a stateA handler that starts on entry and stops on exit.
Wait in a statethen next on delayed(source, 2)A library source that starts counting when the state enters.
Organize several levelsNested ~> cases or named machinesA child state, or independent state axes with a shared lifetime.

States and the transitions between them

A named machine is written like a function whose body is its cases. ~> after the name marks that body, as ~ marks a pattern function. The machine exposes its state as a union-valued declaration, and a machine declared in a class gives each instance its own state:

  • Read the state: Use the familiar union case test. A new door starts closed.
  • Publish an event: Request a transition through the door's event.
  • Observe the result: The transition finishes before the publishing call returns, so the next read sees open.
  • Initial state: The first case without a trigger starts active.
  • Outgoing transitions: Each then belongs to the state enclosing it, so an open request matters while closed and a close request matters while open.
. door = Door()
-- door.phase is .closed
door.open-requests <- true
-- door.phase is .open

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Door

+ event open-requests Bool
+ event close-requests Bool

────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> closed
    then open on open-requests

~> open
    then closed on close-requests

Both lines print true. Transitions triggered by a declared event run to completion before the publication returns: the event's ordinary handlers run first, then the machine's transitions. When a transition's actions publish further events, the transitions those events trigger wait until the current one finishes, then run in order, still before the outermost publication returns. A machine is therefore never inside two transitions at once, and a loop that publishes an event on every step sees each machine's new state on the next line. A source with its own delivery timing, such as AsyncChannel, triggers transitions when it delivers.

~> declares a case and can also attach a trigger that enters it. A trigger on a case at the machine's root is available throughout that machine's active lifetime. A then inside a case instead describes an outgoing transition from that case. Use that placement to express which events are meaningful in each state.

An untriggered case is a destination, not an instruction to advance to the next line. The door stays closed until a transition selects open; it does not run through both declarations.

Events can carry the next state's data

The for part of a transition uses structural patterns. It can recognize a union case or tuple and capture values. A following when guard can use those captures; the target's arguments become its payload.

  • Recognize and capture: Only a .entered submission matches, and its string becomes name.
  • Guard the transition: The capture is available before the guard runs.
  • Carry data forward: Store the accepted name with the state.
  • Read the result: Matching the machine extracts the payload. This prints Accepted Ada.
+ submitted AsyncChannel'Submission

+ form ~>
    ~> waiting
    ~> accepted(name) for .entered(name) on submitted when name.length > 0
    ~> rejected for .entered(name) on submitted when name.length == 0

submitted <- .entered("Ada")
do new
    -- match form
        | .accepted(name)
            "Accepted $name"
        ??
            "No accepted name"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Submission is Union

| entered String

The incoming event and the machine's state are separate values. Submission describes what arrived; the inferred state union describes what the form is doing as a result. Several payload expressions can be supplied as a tuple, as in authenticating(email, password). Sum types explains the ordinary case tests and matches used to read them.

For a simple guard without destructuring, each names the arriving item:

~> positive on numbers when each > 0

Sibling transitions sharing a trigger source are tried in source order. The first matching pattern and guard wins for that decision. Without a matching transition or a fallback, that decision leaves the active state unchanged. Put a more specific alternative before a broad one when both could accept the same event.

Immediate decisions and event decisions

if decides when the owning machine or state enters. when filters an arriving event. They are useful at different moments:

  • Entry decision: The machine enters guest, then immediately selects member because access is available.
  • Later change: Changing the condition's input does not itself rerun the entry decision. Both reads print true.
+ has-access = true

+ access ~>
    ~> guest
    ~> member if has-access

-- access is .member
has-access = false
-- access is .member

An immediate decision can also match a shape, using a form such as then ready(value) if | .available(value) = result. As with event decisions, source order resolves competing immediate transitions. A then with no trigger always passes, so a final then wandering after a list of if decisions names where the state goes when none of them match. Immediate decisions cannot lead back to a state that is still being entered, because entering would never settle; the compiler rejects such a loop, and a trigger such as on delayed(ticks, 1) is how a state comes back around.

To respond to later changes, supply a source of events or updates. A Boolean expression in an if trigger is not a continuously observed condition. The stream and tracked-value forms in Concurrency and reactivity provide the vocabulary for changing sources.

Entry, exit, and the lifetime of a state

A state body can contain entry actions, exit actions, local bindings, and continuations. do runs on entry; do finally runs when that activation exits:

  • Enter: The initial activation prints enter showing.
  • Exit: Leaving the activation prints exit showing.
  • Enter again: A transition back to the same state exits it and starts a fresh activation. Refresh therefore prints the exit line followed by another entry line.
+ refresh AsyncChannel'Bool

+ view ~>
    ~> showing
        do
            -- "enter showing"

        do finally
            -- "exit showing"

        then showing on refresh

refresh <- true
do new
    -- view is .showing

The final line prints true. A self-transition is a restart of the state's lifetime, so use it when entry work and local state should be recreated. An ordinary update inside an action does not require a transition.

Immediate locals (.) and lazy locals (..) belong to an activation. Re-entering recreates them; repeated reads of a lazy local within one activation reuse that activation's value. Continuations can use the state's event captures and local sources.

State-owned transition subscriptions are removed on exit. Callbacks belonging to an old activation cannot advance a later activation of that state. This is useful for a request that becomes obsolete when a user cancels or leaves a screen. It does not mean all independent work behind a source is canceled: the producer's resource and task lifetime still needs its own completion or cancellation arrangement.

Work while a state is active

A for … on handler inside a state runs for each arrival while that state is active. It subscribes when the state enters and stops when the state exits. Every source a state names is evaluated on entry, so a source with its own state starts fresh each time. Timers are ordinary library sources built this way: in /stream/timing, delayed(source, limit) forwards arrivals once their payloads add up to the limit, and totaled(source) delivers each arrival paired with the running total. Together they let a fixed-step loop drive a machine without counters in the class:

  • Handle arrivals: While heating, every tick adds heat.
  • Wait for the total: Four half-second ticks add up to the limit, so the kettle starts whistling on the fourth tick.
  • Stop on exit: Later ticks no longer reach the handler. This prints true and 20.
/stream/timing

. kettle = Kettle()
for i in 0 .. < 6
    kettle.ticks <- 0.5
-- kettle.phase is .whistling
-- kettle.heat

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Kettle

+ event ticks F64
+ heat F64 = 0

────────────────────
+ phase ~>

~> heating
    for dt on ticks
        heat += dt * 10

    then whistling on delayed(ticks, 2)

~> whistling

Handlers run with the machine's transitions, after the event's ordinary handlers. Work from a source that relays an event, like delayed(ticks, 2), waits the same way. A state's handlers and transitions take each arrival in source order, so a transition written before a handler can leave the state before that handler sees the arrival. A when clause filters arrivals the same way it does for a transition. A handler's pattern binds the arrival as it does for any for … on subscription.

A timer belongs to the state that names it: the state enclosing a then or a handler, or the machine itself for a trigger on a root case. Re-entering that state, including through a self-transition, starts the total again from zero, while a parent's timer keeps counting as its children change. Once delayed starts forwarding, the transition checks its guard on each arrival, so a guard that is false holds the transition until a later arrival passes it. A handler that needs the time spent in its state reads it from totaled: for elapsed, dt on totaled(ticks).

Nested states share a parent lifetime

Nested cases describe a more specific state inside an active parent. Entering a child leaves the parent active:

  • Parent: The outer machine starts in editing.
  • Child: Its initial child is focused. Both case tests are true at once.
  • Leave the parent: Finishing exits the active child before the parent and selects done.
+ finish AsyncChannel'Bool

+ editor ~>
    ~> editing
        do finally
            -- "exit editing"

        ~> focused
            do finally
                -- "exit focused"

        then done on finish

    ~> done

-- editor is .editing
-- editor is .focused
finish <- true
do new
    -- editor is .done

The output is true, true, exit focused, exit editing, and true. Sibling cases are alternatives, but a parent and its active descendant describe different levels of the same configuration. A machine with nested states therefore has more structure than a single flat union tag. Use its case tests to ask which levels are active.

Re-entering a parent exits and rebuilds its active subtree. Leaving it also exits any named machines declared inside it and removes their transition subscriptions.

Independent state axes

Some choices should vary independently. A session can be authenticated while its network is offline. Declare separate named machines inside a shared parent instead of enumerating every combination. This fragment assumes signed-in and connected event sources:

+ session ~>
    ~> running
        + identity ~>
            ~> guest
            ~> member on signed-in

        + network ~>
            ~> offline
            ~> online on connected

Changing identity does not select a case in network, and both belong to the lifetime of running. Use nested cases for successive levels of one state and nested named machines for independent choices.

Anonymous machines expose their cases directly

At module level or in class content, a machine can omit the binding name. Yumi then exposes each case as a projection of the machine's state: a Boolean for a case without data, or an optional payload for a case with data.

  • Boolean projection: waiting starts true.
  • Payload projection: received is absent until that case is active.
  • Read the payload: After the transition, this prints hello.
+ messages AsyncChannel'String

~> waiting
~> received(value) for value on messages

-- waiting
-- received == null
messages <- "hello"
do new
    -- received ?? "No message"
    -- waiting

This prints true, true, hello, and false. The generated names describe one machine; they are not unrelated mutable flags. An anonymous machine with only triggered cases can start inactive, with every projection false or absent, until a trigger selects a case.

Choose the declaration's location according to who owns it:

DeclarationOwnership and observation
Module-level + phase ~>A module-owned named machine, read with case tests or matches.
Class + phase ~>Independent machine storage for every object.
Local . phase ~>A machine initialized when execution reaches the declaration.
Local .. phase ~>Initialized on first use, once per lazy declaration lifetime.
Anonymous cases in class contentPer-object state with directly readable case projections.

A machine declared in class content, or after a module's thick divider, follows its own thin or thick divider like any function: the header line, a blank line, then the cases at column zero. A machine declared among statements, such as a local, a module's top-level code, or a nested machine inside a state, indents its cases under the header instead, as a local pattern rule does.

A fallback clears its target

The state-machine spelling ?? state has a specific meaning: when the preceding transition decision finds no match, deactivate the named target and its active descendants. It does not enter that state as a default destination.

  • Unmatched decision: The immediate guard is false.
  • Clear the target: Exit loading. Neither state remains active, so both reads print false.
+ is-ready = false

~> loading
    then ready if is-ready
    ?? loading

~> ready

-- loading
-- ready

For event transitions, the fallback belongs to the preceding event decision group and runs when an arrival matches none of that group's alternatives. Omitting the fallback keeps an unmatched decision from clearing state. Use an explicit transition when the desired result is to enter another state.

Let an interface follow the machine

State tests and projections can participate in tracked expressions. Inside a component, markup can read #is-open to follow an anonymous case, or #phase is .open to follow a named machine. A read through another object uses a form such as peer.#is-open.

This class-content fragment assumes a terminal component with open and close event sources:

<This
    <Label
        text = if #is-open then "Open" else "Closed"

~> is-closed
    then is-open on open-requests

~> is-open
    then is-closed on close-requests

The machine owns the transitions; the label declares how the active state appears. Styles can use the same tracked values. Markup and stylesheets explains the surrounding tree and live-property model.

Use a state machine when the program has meaningful phases, phase-specific events, or work whose lifetime belongs to a phase. Use an ordinary union when a value only needs to describe an alternative, and a subscription when each arrival can be handled without a state model. The benefit of the machine is making the allowed progress and its lifetimes visible together.

Errors

Yumi separates recoverable errors from panics. A recoverable error is an alternative to a function's successful result. It normally propagates through callers until some code chooses to handle it. A panic interrupts execution by unwinding through the active calls and their cleanup blocks.

Both use ?! to signal failure, but the type of the value determines which mechanism applies. An ordinary subtype of Error uses the recoverable error path. Panic and its subtypes use the panic path.

At a glance

SituationMechanism
A function cannot produce its normal answerReturn a recoverable error with ?!
A caller cannot recover locallyLet the error propagate
A caller can supply a replacement valueAttach a catch handler
A caller needs to inspect success and failureHold the result with prefix catch
Failure should mean absenceUse catch?
An invariant is broken and execution must unwindRaise a Panic
Work must happen when a scope exitsRegister do finally cleanup

Declaring and producing errors

Define an error by deriving a class from Error. A function signature can name its successful result followed by the recoverable errors it may return:

  • Error type: Define a recoverable failure with a message and any domain-specific fields.
  • Result contract: Return an integer on success or OddNumber on failure.
  • Conditional failure: Return the error when the condition is true; skip the division.
  • Hold the outcome: Allow the error to become a printable value. The calls print 5 and Expected an even number.
-- half(10)
-- catch half(3)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ OddNumber is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ half Int ?! OddNumber
    - value Int

?! OddNumber("Expected an even number")
    if value % 2 != 0

value / 2

Error provides a message, an optional source location, and an optional previous error for preserving a chain of causes. Its ordinary string conversion displays the message. Custom error classes can add data that callers need to distinguish or explain a failure.

Multiple error types are written as repeated declarations. This signature fragment describes a successful String or either of two errors:

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ read-config String ?! FileNotFound ?! PermissionDenied
    - path String

Only recoverable Error subtypes belong in these declarations. ?! Int is invalid, and ?! Panic cannot be declared as a recoverable error channel.

Automatic propagation

At an ordinary call site, use the successful result directly. If the call produces an error, the containing computation exits through its error path instead:

-- adjusted-count(true)
-- catch adjusted-count(false)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ CountUnavailable is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-count Int ?! CountUnavailable
    - available Bool

if available
    = 41
?! CountUnavailable("Count unavailable")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ adjusted-count Int ?! CountUnavailable
    - available Bool

read-count(available) + 1
  • Produce an error: The unavailable branch cannot supply the count.
  • Propagate automatically: Add only on success; an error exits the computation without a call-site propagation marker.
  • Boundary contract: Declare the error that may escape. The calls print 42 and Count unavailable.

Propagation does not undo earlier work. If a function changes state before a later operation fails, those changes remain unless the program explicitly compensates for them. Cleanup is a separate responsibility, described below.

Yumi can infer recoverable errors in functions without explicit error declarations. When a function declares its error channels, the compiler checks that escaping errors fit them. An unhandled error outside that contract must be declared, handled, or transformed.

  • API boundaries: explicit error declarations communicate what callers should handle.
  • Recursion: an error channel may need a declaration before recursive calls establish the return convention.
  • Interfaces: implementations must respect the interface's error contract.

Holding a result with catch

Prefix catch turns off automatic propagation for the expression it holds. The result retains both possibilities: a successful value or an error. This held result is often called a Result. Match it to decide what to do:

  • Retain both outcomes: Prefix catch disables automatic propagation for the held expression.
  • Success arm: Bind the string directly; no Ok wrapper is needed.
  • Error arm: Choose a policy using the typed error. Here the output is Cannot greet: No name was supplied.
. result = catch read-name(false)
-- match result
    | name String
        "Hello, $name"
    | error NameUnavailable
        "Cannot greet: ${error.message}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ NameUnavailable is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-name String ?! NameUnavailable
    - available Bool

if available
    = "Yumi"
?! NameUnavailable("No name was supplied")

An ordinary match must cover the result's success and error possibilities, either explicitly or through a suitable fallback. Handling one error type does not cover other error types. A broad Error pattern can cover recoverable error alternatives when they deliberately share one policy.

Holding an error is not itself recovery. It keeps the decision in the current computation. That decision might be to log it, use a fallback, retry, or explicitly propagate it with ?! error.

Recovering with attached handlers

An attached catch handles selected errors from the expression directly above it. Its body can supply the value to use instead of the failed expression's result:

-- display-name(false)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ NameUnavailable is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-name String ?! NameUnavailable
    - available Bool

if available
    = "Yumi"
?! NameUnavailable("No name was supplied")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ display-name String
    - available Bool

read-name(available)
    catch NameUnavailable
        "Guest"
  • Attached recovery: Keep a successful string or replace this specific failure with "Guest".
  • Inspect the error: write catch error NameUnavailable to give it a local name.
  • Distinguish failures: attach additional handlers for additional types.
  • Order overlapping handlers: put a specific subtype before a broad handler when their policies differ.

Errors not handled by an attached handler still propagate automatically. Handling FileNotFound, for example, does not silently discard PermissionDenied.

This is different from prefix catch. Prefix catch holds the result and disables that automatic propagation. If you combine prefix holding with attached handlers, the original error alternatives must all be accounted for; unhandled alternatives are not implicitly sent to the caller.

A handler can also use ?! ReplacementError("...") to propagate a different error immediately. The explicit ?! matters: constructing an error object as an ordinary handler value does not by itself mean “leave this function now.”

Turning failure into absence with catch?

Use catch? when the error details are intentionally irrelevant. It keeps a successful value and converts a recoverable error into absence:

-- catch? read-count(true) ?? 0
-- catch? read-count(false) ?? 0

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ CountUnavailable is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-count Int ?! CountUnavailable
    - available Bool

if available
    = 41
?! CountUnavailable("Count unavailable")
  • Keep success: A successful call prints 41.
  • Discard failure details: Convert the error into absence, then use 0. A successful zero or false would still be present.

This is concise, but it discards the error's identity and explanation. Use an attached handler or a held result when different failures require different treatment. A fallback should be a deliberate policy, not merely a way to make an error disappear.

Neither catch nor catch? is the panic-recovery mechanism. They operate on recoverable error results.

Translating errors and retaining their cause

A function may want to expose a domain-specific error instead of the lower-level error it encounters. An error transformer declares that mapping in the function body:

  • Translate at the boundary: Map an escaping IOError to LoadError; this declaration does not fail unconditionally.
  • Retain the cause: The original error stays available through previous. The output is Could not load settings: Disk unavailable.
. result = catch load()
-- match result
    | value Int
        "Loaded $value"
    | error LoadError
        "${error.message}: ${error.previous}"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ LoadError is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-value Int ?! IOError

?! IOError("Disk unavailable")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do load Int ?! LoadError

?! LoadError("Could not load settings")
    catch error IOError

= read-value()

Transformation lets each layer describe a failure in its own terms without losing the cause. The resulting chain can be inspected through previous. A transformer can also match a cause chain; this fragment matches a ConfigError whose previous error is an IOError:

?! LoadError("Could not load settings")
    catch config ConfigError <- io IOError

Transformer expressions must not call functions that return recoverable errors. The mapping must not introduce another unresolved failure while translating the original one. Unlike ordinary attached handlers, overlapping transformers for the same error chain are rejected as ambiguous.

Cleanup with do finally

Register cleanup with do finally. Its body runs when the enclosing scope exits, including normal completion, a return, recoverable error propagation, or panic unwinding:

  • Register an exit action: Run cleanup on normal completion, return, error propagation, or panic unwinding.
  • Successful exit: Cleanup runs before the caller receives 7.
  • Error exit: Cleanup also runs before the caller receives the error.
-- perform(true)
-- catch perform(false)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ WorkFailed is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do perform Int ?! WorkFailed
    - succeeds Bool

do finally
    -- "cleanup"

if succeeds
    = 7
?! WorkFailed("Work failed")

The output is:

cleanup
7
cleanup
Work failed

Cleanup runs before the caller receives either outcome. Multiple cleanup blocks in the same scope run in reverse registration order. A cleanup registered inside a nested block belongs to that block's scope, rather than necessarily waiting for the entire function to finish.

Place cleanup registration after the resource it protects has been acquired. do finally provides an exit action; it does not automatically roll back a transaction or restore state changed earlier in the function.

Panics and recovery

Use ?! Panic("...") for the separate unwinding path. Runtime failures such as out-of-bounds access can also use panic subtypes. Although Panic inherits from Error, it is not a recoverable error alternative in a function's result contract.

A do finally block can call recover() to obtain and recover the active panic:

  • Recover during cleanup: Obtain the active panic, or absence if none is active.
  • Unwind: Take the separate panic path; ordinary catch is not its recovery mechanism.
  • No resumption here: Recovery finishes the function through cleanup. Its caller can then continue.
run()
-- "Caller continued"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do run

do finally
    . panic = recover()
    if panic
        -- "Recovered: $panic"

?! Panic("Broken invariant")
-- "This line is not reached"

Use recovery at a boundary that can make a meaningful decision about a failed operation. Suppressing a panic does not establish that partially modified application state is valid. If the boundary cannot continue safely, it can let unwinding continue rather than recover, or recover and raise another panic.

An unhandled recoverable error or panic reaching the top-level execution boundary is reported as a failure, with diagnostic context such as its message and stack trace. Automatic propagation is not automatic success and does not silently discard an unhandled error.

Choosing an error policy

Use a recoverable error when callers should be able to make an ordinary decision about a failure. Use a panic for a failure that needs the unwinding mechanism, such as a violated invariant. Choose based on how callers should respond, rather than simply how serious the message sounds.

At each boundary:

  1. Choose whether to propagate, replace the value, inspect the result, or translate the error.
  2. Keep error types specific enough to support that decision.
  3. Use catch? only when losing the explanation is acceptable.
  4. Arrange cleanup independently of the chosen error policy.

Markup and stylesheets

Yumi can describe an object tree directly in source. Markup names the objects, their properties, and their children; stylesheets collect rules for their appearance and layout; reactive expressions connect them to changing state.

This makes interfaces part of the language's expression vocabulary. The program can describe a tree in the same source language as its data model, event handlers, and computations.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Tree structure< creates nodes; indentation groups children.
PropertiesAssign ordinary values and expressions.
Content compositionSlots accept caller-supplied content; branches and repetition follow data.
Styles• introduces styling; named rules collect shared decisions.
Live behaviorTracked state, events, and subscriptions connect the tree to the application.
TargetsTerminal and graphical libraries supply concrete controls and rendering.
