The shape of the source follows the tree

This fragment uses the terminal library's boxes and labels:

  • Object node: Construct a box with identity, properties, and behavior.
  • Layout and spacing: Introduce style information beside the node.
  • Children: Indentation places two labels inside the box; their text is a constructor argument.
<Box • flex-col p:1
    <Label "Account"
    <Label "Ready" • text:green

Markup constructs objects. A node can have identity, expose properties, participate in events, and own resources. This is distinct from a text template that produces a string containing tags. A node's type remains connected to ordinary Yumi declarations and behavior.

The tree form removes much of the visual overhead of allocating objects one at a time and then connecting parent and child references. It also makes the nesting visible where a reader is deciding how the interface is composed.

Properties remain expressions

Property assignments can use ordinary Yumi values and expressions. This fragment illustrates the graphical library's window markup:

  • Property assignment: Supply an ordinary string value.
  • Structured value: Properties use Yumi expressions, including tuples.
  • Nested object: The window also owns child content.
<Window
    title = "Report"
    size = (720, 480)
    background = "#f7f7f9"

    <Box • absolute cover:.parent

The markup is not a separate configuration language with its own limited calculation rules. A property's value can come from the same functions and types used elsewhere in the program. Likewise, behavior can live in ordinary methods instead of becoming a large inline block inside the tree.

Composition includes content

Composition featureWhat it lets a component do
SlotsAccept caller-supplied content, such as a dialog body and actions
Slot forwardingPass content through an intermediate component
Conditional markupChoose the branch that matches application state
Repeated markupConstruct children from a collection of domain values

The component owns the surrounding structure, layout, and behavior. The caller supplies the pieces that vary.

Styles collect decisions that belong together

Style shorthands make common combinations concise:

<Box • flex-row p:1 border-rounded border:aqua
<Label "Ready" • bg:blue text:white
  • Arrangement: Keep layout and spacing close to the affected node.
  • Border: Combine shorthands for shape and color.
  • Colors: Style the label's background and text.

Here layout, spacing, border, and color decisions remain close to the relevant node. Reusable rules can move repeated choices into a stylesheet. This declaration fragment defines a named style in a context that supplies the corresponding properties and shorthands:

• status-panel • flex-col p:1 bg:black

A node can then refer to status-panel in its style list. Stylesheets can group and extend rules, while selectors and state-dependent rules let appearance follow the role and state of nodes in the tree.

The advantage grows when the same components appear throughout an application. A common style can express a shared decision once, while a particular component can retain the properties that are specific to its own behavior.

State can stay connected to the declaration

An interface needs to change after it is created. Tracked reads identify the values that a live expression depends on. For example, a property assignment can read #title so that the declaration participates in changes to the title, rather than merely taking an initial copy.

Streams can supply changing values too. Latest-value expressions make the current value of a stream available to a live calculation. That connects network results, application events, and state changes to the same expression system.

This does not remove the need to decide who owns state. A component should have a clear relationship to the values it changes and the subscriptions it creates. The payoff is that much of the display can remain a declaration of how that state should appear.

Concurrency and reactivity explains the tracked-value and subscription model separately from its use in a user interface.

State machines organize behavior around named phases and the events that move between them. Their state tests and case projections can drive tracked properties and styles, keeping a component's appearance connected to its current phase.

Events connect the tree to behavior

Nodes can publish events and subscribe to other nodes' events. A parent component can own selection, command routing, or dialog behavior while its children focus on displaying data and exposing interactions.

The UI libraries also provide declarative shortcut components. A command's key binding and availability can therefore live in the tree with the controls it affects, instead of requiring a second, disconnected description of the interface.

Things to decide:

  • Which component owns state and may change it?
  • Who owns each event subscription?
  • What stops an obsolete node from influencing state after removal?

Markup composition, reactive ownership, and resource cleanup belong to the same component design.

Terminal and graphical applications

Yumi's terminal and graphical libraries share these language ideas while supplying different rendering and input facilities. Terminal components include forms, lists, trees, tables, editors, and dialogs. Graphical components provide windows, controls, layout, and drawing.

Sharing a declarative vocabulary does not imply that every control or platform feature is identical. It means the reader can carry the same model of object trees, state, styles, and events between application domains.

The broader library tour is in Batteries included. The distinctive language feature is the connection: the tree's structure, its changing values, and the code that reacts to it all belong to Yumi.

Modules, native code, and memory

Yumi's expression-oriented surface sits on a native foundation. Programs are organized into modules, compiled to native code, and able to call C libraries. Garbage collection handles ordinary object memory, while explicit storage facilities provide more control for code with a different lifetime or layout requirement.

These capabilities let a program use high-level models without treating operating-system interfaces and data representation as somebody else's problem.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
ModulesBare-path imports, visibility markers, and executable module bodies.
Native compilationConcrete uses guide specialization, inlining, and other optimizations.
C bridgeHeaders, native functions and data, pointers, and callbacks.
Managed memoryGarbage collection for ordinary object relationships.
Explicit storageArenas, backing storage, and GC-free regions for specific lifetime requirements.
Language toolingSource, syntax-tree, type-analysis, and compiler facilities.

Modules use paths directly

Imports are bare paths at the beginning of a source file:

  • Library modules: Absolute module paths identify declarations through Yumi's module lookup.
  • Nearby module: Resolve a module relative to the current file. Public + and private _ declarations control exposure.
/net/http
/net/url
./response

A module can contain executable code as well as declarations. Small programs can therefore begin with their work directly, without introducing a special entry-point function merely to call another function. A larger module can define types and helpers and keep its top-level work small.

Top-level execution is convenient, but initialization is still behavior. Import relationships, global state, and effects should remain understandable as a program grows. A module that mainly supplies reusable declarations has a different role from one that starts an application.

Compilation follows the program's use of declarations

Yumi compiles to native code. Its toolchain includes its own native-code machinery rather than using LLVM as its compiler backend. On-demand compilation lets the compiler work from the declarations and concrete uses needed by the program.

That is especially relevant to generics and overloads. Source declarations describe families of operations; a particular program supplies concrete combinations of types and calls. Whole-program information gives the compiler opportunities to specialize, inline, and remove intermediate machinery.

An abstraction's appearance in source does not dictate one fixed runtime representation. A composed stream operation may be fused with its consumer, while a generator that escapes and resumes independently may need stored state. The intended behavior remains the contract; the compiler can choose how to realize it.

Native compilation does not by itself mean that a program has no runtime support. Tasks, garbage collection, IO, and other facilities have runtime responsibilities. Likewise, platform integration still depends on which backend and library facilities are available for that platform.

The C bridge reaches existing native libraries

Yumi can import C declarations through headers and call them through its C namespace. This fragment shows the shape of a C-library use:

  • C declarations: Import the header that supplies the foreign declaration.
  • C namespace: Call the native function with a value supplied by the surrounding program.
/stdlib.h

C:abs(value)

The bridge includes native function and data types, pointers, and the declarations needed to interoperate with existing APIs. It lets a Yumi library wrap an operating-system or third-party facility and expose an interface suited to ordinary Yumi code.

A native wrapper should settle these questions near the bridge:

ConcernContract to expose
RepresentationHow Yumi values map to native data
OwnershipWhether a pointer is borrowed, owned, or managed by another library
LifetimeWhen an allocation or handle must be released
FailureHow native failure becomes an ordinary Yumi outcome
CallbacksHow long native code can retain the callback and its captured state

Garbage collection is the ordinary memory model

Yumi normally manages object memory with garbage collection. Values can be retained by data structures and shared between parts of a program without requiring every function signature to describe a manual allocation protocol.

Memory reachability is not the same thing as resource ownership. A socket, file, subscription, or worker can need an explicit end to its activity even when the language manages the memory of its wrapper. Cleanup belongs to the operation or component that owns that resource.

Errors covers do finally and cleanup during exits. The stream and concurrency chapters describe the corresponding lifetime decisions for traversals and producers.

Explicit memory for explicit lifetimes

Storage choiceUseful whenObligation
Garbage-collected objectsValues have shared, interdependent lifetimesAvoid unwanted retention
Arena-backed dataMany values belong to one computationDo not use values after the arena is released
Native allocation or handleA foreign API owns the representationFollow that API's release and borrowing rules

Builders and collections can use storage appropriate to their owner.

This can make temporary compiler data, parsing work, or other bounded computations easier to reason about as a group. It also creates an obligation: values backed by that storage must not be used after the storage is released. Raw pointers and native interoperation require similarly explicit reasoning.

Yumi also has facilities for expressing GC-free regions of implementation. These are useful when avoiding garbage-collected allocation is an actual requirement, rather than a preference that should shape every ordinary helper.

Collections and data layout surveys arrays, views, bitmaps, and tables. Their purpose is complementary: one decision concerns how long storage exists, and another concerns how the values are arranged within it.

Language tooling is part of the project

Yumi's library includes parsing, syntax-tree, type-analysis, and compiler-related facilities, with ongoing self-hosted compiler work. These make the language itself a domain that Yumi programs can work on. A language guide can show that capability without requiring readers to learn the compiler's internal passes.

The combination is useful to evaluate as a whole: a program can begin with ordinary modules, types, and managed objects, then reach native APIs or choose a more explicit storage model where the problem calls for one.

Probes and observability

Yumi includes probes for observing a running program. A probe can record that something happened, expose a value, group related activity, or make an object available for inspection. The goal is to preserve useful context about execution instead of reducing every observation to an isolated line of text.

This matters particularly for programs with tasks, streams, and live interfaces. The question is often not just what value was returned, but which task produced it, what the object was doing, and what happened before another component stopped making progress.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Event / valueRecord what happened and the data that explains it.
GroupsConnect the beginning and end of related activity.
Object identityFollow one request or component across modules and tasks.
Snapshot / live inspectionInspect recorded state or a still-present object.
Counters / profilingMeasure frequency and accumulated work.
SelectionEnable relevant observations without relying on them for application behavior.

Observations have a place in the source

A probe names an observation at the point where it helps explain the program. Here the application computes a value, then exposes it to an enabled probe:

  • Application work: Compute the value independently of whether observation is enabled.
  • Named probe: Associate the observation with http.value and this source location.
  • Observed value: Expose 42 to the selected probe. The print remains ordinary application behavior.
. value = 21 * 2
//http.value -> value
-- value

The // form is executable probe notation. Choose names at the level that explains the work: a parser might record recognized records, while a channel implementation records waiting readers.

Observation can be selected

Probe selection lets an investigation focus on a relevant area. A program can contain useful instrumentation without every run collecting every possible observation. Probe-only expressions are not ordinary application work that should be relied upon to run when the probe is disabled.

This distinction allows an observation to include a derived value without making that value part of the program's result. It also means effects required by the application belong in ordinary code, not hidden inside an optional observation.

The useful design goal is to keep probes near the event they explain while retaining control over what an investigation records.

Objects make a timeline easier to interpret

An object identity can connect observations that occur far apart in the source. A request might be created in one module, queued in another, and completed by a task elsewhere. Seeing those observations as one request's history is more informative than matching text by eye.

Snapshots expose state at a point in time. Inspection support can also make information available from a live object when the runtime and object provide the relevant capability. For a channel, useful state might include buffered values, waiting activity, or subscriptions.

The distinction between a snapshot and live inspection matters. One describes what was recorded at an earlier point; the other asks about an object that is still present. A useful tool should make the origin and time of that information visible.

Counts and durations answer different questions

EvidenceQuestion it answers
Event traceIn what order did the work happen?
CounterHow often did an operation run?
Duration / profileWhere did time or work accumulate?
SnapshotWhat state existed at the recorded moment?
Live inspectionWhat can the object report now?

Group boundaries and counters can describe a batch without recording every item as a large snapshot:

  • Begin a group: Associate the following activity with one processing group.
  • Count work: An enabled counter advances for each visited item.
  • End the group: Mark completion of the related activity.
//+batch.process
for value in [10, 20, 30]
    //batch.items ++
    -- value
//-batch.process

Probe names and object associations connect measurements to the program's concepts. The profile example in the repository uses the same group and counter forms for parsing and rendering work.

Following a stream through the program

Consider a producer writing work into a channel and a consumer updating an interface. Useful observations might be:

  1. A work item is created, with its identity and input size.
  2. The item is queued, together with the channel's current state.
  3. A task begins processing it.
  4. The result is published.
  5. A component accepts the result or ignores it because its state has changed.

Those observations can explain a delay that would be difficult to locate with only the producer's input and the final display. They also separate waiting from processing and publication from consumption.

The chapter on Concurrency and reactivity explains the behaviors these observations describe. Probes provide a way to inspect those behaviors in a particular run.

Observation is still work

  • Choose the scope. Large snapshots and frequent events have different costs from occasional counters.
  • Account for instrumentation. Collection uses time and storage; interpret measurements with the enabled observations in mind.
  • Keep expectations separate. Tests establish expected behavior. A trace explains one run and does not guarantee the same ordering in every run.

For someone evaluating Yumi, the significant capability is that observation has language and runtime support. Tasks, objects, and streams can remain recognizable in the evidence collected about them, rather than disappearing behind a wall of unrelated print statements.

Batteries included

Yumi includes libraries for data, files, networks, graphics, interfaces, and the language itself. The useful part is how they connect: HTTP bodies supply streams, patterns recognize records, units describe time and geometry, and reactive values feed interfaces.

This is a capability map, not an inventory of every function.

At a glance

AreaCapabilitiesModules
Collections and streamsLists, maps, arrays, builders, tables, bitmaps; selection, aggregation, combination, buffering, sorting/core, /stream
Files and storageFiles, databases, persistent lists, B-trees/file/file, /file/db, /file/dblist, /file/btree
Host environmentArguments, environment, paths, processes, signals/os/cli, /os/env, /os/path, /os/process, /os/signal
Time and quantitiesDurations, timestamps, dates, clocks, timers, zones, mathematics, units/time, /math, /units
FormatsJSON, CSV, Markdown, binary input/data/json, /data/csv, /data/markdown, /data/stream
NetworkingDNS, TCP/TLS sockets, URLs, HTTP, WebSockets, server-sent events, API helpers, JSON-RPC/net, /api, /data/jsonrpc
AIModels, conversations, media, streaming responses, OpenAI integration/ai, /ai/model, /ai/chat, /ai/media, /ai/openai/completions
GraphicsGeometry, colors, paths, curves, drawing, text, layers/graphics
Terminal UILayout, controls, editors, dialogs, focus, shortcuts, themes/tui
Graphical UIApplications, windows, controls, input, scenes, drawing integration/gui
Testing and observationTest cases, result presentation, probes, inspection, counters, profiling/test, /core/probes
Language toolingSource, syntax trees, declarations, types, lint, compiler representations/lang

Collections and stream processing

Stored data and ongoing work use the same sequence vocabulary. A consumer can filter records, retain a running total, or collect a finite result without prescribing where the items came from.

  • Focused import: Bring in the aggregation operations.
  • Running result: Start from zero and emit each updated accumulator.
  • Combination: Add each input. Collecting the results produces 2, 5, 9.
/stream/aggregate

. totals = scan(0, [2, 3, 4]) • using :: total, item => total + item
-- List(totals)
  • Storage: lists, maps, ranges, arrays, immutable storage, builders, bitmaps, and tables.
  • Processing: aggregate, filter, combine, coincidence, inspect, router, and sort groups under /stream.
  • Choose deliberately: some operations need the whole input; others retain only an accumulator or nearby items.

See Collections and data layout and Stream pipelines.

Files and persistent storage

NeedBuilding block
Read or write a documentFile access and byte/text input
Decode file contentsFormat libraries or stream patterns
Retain application data across runsDatabase and persistent-list facilities
Organize lookup and updatesB-tree support

File streams and persistent structures solve different problems: one supplies input to a computation; the other retains and organizes data for later use.

Operating-system integration

A command-line tool can work with arguments, environment variables, paths, processes, and signals. The C bridge reaches native facilities beyond those wrappers.

  • Parse the command's inputs with /os/cli.
  • Read environment and resolve paths with /os/env and /os/path.
  • Coordinate other processes and host signals with /os/process and /os/signal.

Time, mathematics, and units

Time facilities distinguish elapsed quantities from calendar concepts. Durations, timestamps, dates, clocks, timers, and zones have different jobs.

  • Typed time: The connected units convert milliseconds to seconds.
  • Include the unit: Format the value with its canonical suffix.
/time/duration

. timeout Seconds = 1500ms
-- timeout as UnitString

Mathematics and unit families also support angles, distances, graphics coordinates, and layout. See Numerical units for conversion rules and their limits.

Text, structured data, and binary input

Format or taskCapability
JSONExchange API payloads and structured files
CSVMove tabular data into ordinary collections
MarkdownConsume formatted text
Binary streamsDecode fields whose byte order and representation matter
Custom formatUse stream patterns to write a grammar
Decoded valuesUse structural patterns to recognize fields and shapes

Each format module defines its actual coverage; the presence of a format name does not imply every variant is supported. For authored output, string templates keep the document visible while expressions supply its changing parts.

Networking and APIs

Networking spans request-and-response work and longer-lived connections:

  • Connect: DNS, URLs, and TCP or TLS-backed sockets.
  • Request: HTTP and JSON API helpers.
  • Follow arrivals: WebSockets and server-sent events.
  • Exchange structured calls: JSON-RPC facilities.

Waiting passes through ordinary helpers. This fragment assumes imports from /net/http and a URL named url:

  • Call the helper: Use ordinary call syntax.
  • Declare the helper: There is no async marker.
  • Wait inside it: The request can suspend for network IO without adding await at either call.
-- page-body(url)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ page-body String
    - url URL

page.text

.. page = http-get(url)

Client/server roles, transport options, and protocol coverage are contracts of the particular module. See Concurrency and reactivity for waiting and task behavior.

AI applications

The AI libraries connect models, conversations, media, and streaming responses. The supplied OpenAI integration implements provider-specific behavior.

A chat interface brings together:

  1. A conversation model and request.
  2. Incremental response data.
  3. A live display that updates as results arrive.

Shared abstractions do not imply identical provider support for every media or response feature.

Geometry and graphics

AreaCapabilities
GeometryPoints, vectors, matrices, shapes, curves, intersections, polygons
Path operationsBoolean operations, offsets, strokes, transformations
RenderingColors, canvases, drawing, text, layers, artwork

Geometry can be useful in a data-processing program on its own. Rendering adds platform integration. Units and operator overloads let domain relationships appear directly in expressions.

Terminal applications

The /tui family supplies controls with layout, input, and state:

  • Structure: boxes, forms, dialogs, lists, trees, tables.
  • Content and editing: labels, buttons, text editing, progress displays, status areas.
  • Interaction: keyboard shortcuts, focus, scrolling.
  • Presentation: themes and styles.

Components use markup and reactive state. See Markup and stylesheets for the shared declarative model.

Graphical applications

The /gui family works with /graphics to provide applications, windows, controls, layout, input, styles, scenes, and drawing integration.

The same object-tree model carries over from terminal applications. Concrete controls and rendering remain library-specific. The current implementation includes macOS-native and Metal-related facilities; platform support is part of evaluating what you can build today.

Testing and observation

GoalSupport
State expected behaviorTest cases and result presentation in /test
Explain a particular runEvents, values, object inspection, counters, and profiling in /core/probes

Observations can retain the object and task context needed to understand channels and UI state. See Probes and observability.

Language tooling

The /lang family works with source, syntax trees, declarations, types, lint, and compiler representations. It underpins the project's self-hosted language work.

These facilities make Yumi itself a domain for Yumi programs. They include internal machinery; not every compiler representation is a stable extension API.

The value of including the pieces together

A network response can feed a stream grammar. Its records can become union values, pass through a pipeline, and update a declarative interface. Probes can follow the objects through that work.

The shared models matter as much as the breadth: values, sequences, state, and behavior remain recognizable across library boundaries.

Why Yumi looks the way it does

I made several choices in Yumi that are likely to look strange on first contact. Some remove familiar punctuation. Others add punctuation where most languages use words. A few take things normally left to a style guide and make them part of the grammar.

The thread connecting these choices is how I want source code to read. I want declarations to have an obvious outline, names to look like words, and expressions to put their main idea where the eye arrives first. I am willing to spend more vertical space to make those relationships visible.

That is a preference, not a claim that unfamiliar syntax is inherently better. Familiarity is a substantial advantage. Yumi asks readers to give some of it up, and each choice has to earn back that cost.

At a glance

CapabilityWhat it gives you
Visible outlineSignificant dividers, flush-left bodies, one parameter per line.
Reliable name shapesKebab-case values, capitalized types, meaningful operator spaces.
Compact grammarSymbols, apostrophe type arguments, bare-path imports.
Readable relationshipsExpression functions, named arguments, named infix calls.

1. Significant dividers

Horizontal rules are grammar in Yumi. They establish declaration ownership, not just visual separation.

  • Top-level boundary: A thick divider begins the type declaration.
  • Member boundary: A thin divider keeps label inside Token.
  • Next declaration: The next thick divider ends the type's section; double is a module function.
-- Token("hello").label()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Token is Tuple

+ text String

────────────────────
+ label String

"[$text]"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ double Int
    - value Int

value * 2

Compare the notation:

class Token {
    label() {
        return "[" + this.text + "]";
    }
}

function double(value) {
    return value * 2;
}

Why I chose it

  • I want a file's larger divisions visible before I read the words.
  • A conspicuous boundary lets a body sit at the left margin while keeping its owner clear.

Tradeoffs

  • A divider costs a whole line and is less convenient to type than a brace; editor support matters.
  • Changing a thin divider to a thick one changes structure. Fonts, diffs, and copied snippets must preserve the distinction.

2. Kebab case identifiers

Ordinary names use hyphens between words.

  • Word boundaries: Each hyphen belongs to a name; the spaced * is an operator.
. item-count = 3
. unit-price = 20
. total-price = item-count * unit-price
-- total-price

Why I chose it

  • I find total-price easier to read as a compound phrase than totalPrice or total_price.
  • The boundaries are explicit without changing letter height at every word.

Tradeoffs

  • total-price is one identifier; total - price is subtraction. This choice depends on significant spacing.
  • Generic editor word navigation may split at hyphens. Selection, search, and rename need language-aware support.

3. Mandatory identifier case

Capitalization reliably distinguishes everyday Latin type names from value names.

  • Type name: Begin with a capital and use internal capitals as needed.
  • Value name: Use lowercase words separated by hyphens.
. reading = TemperatureReading(21)
-- reading.degrees

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ TemperatureReading is Tuple

+ degrees Int

Why I chose it

  • I want a reader to recognize a name's basic category without finding its declaration.
  • Many languages recommend this distinction. I want both readers and the parser to be able to rely on it.

Tradeoffs

  • Naming freedom becomes a language constraint: temperatureReading is not an ordinary value identifier, and Temperature-Reading is not the type spelling.
  • Acronyms and foreign naming conventions need accommodation. C identifiers use forms such as C:someFunction; supported Greek identifiers have their own rules.

4. Mandatory whitespace around operators

Spaces around ordinary binary operators do grammatical work.

  • One name: Read the hyphenated identifier: 100.
  • Subtraction: Spaces distinguish two operands and an operator: 7.
  • Precedence remains: Multiplication still comes first: 16.
. total = 10
. price = 3
. total-price = 100
-- total-price
-- total - price
-- total + price * 2

In a C-like language, total-price normally subtracts regardless of spacing. That freedom conflicts with the names I want.

Why I chose it

  • Kebab-case names require a predictable distinction between a word and subtraction.
  • I prefer a consistent visual rhythm: solid names, with space around the operations connecting them.

Tradeoffs

  • An edit that looks like formatting can change meaning or invalidate an expression.
  • This is not a universal spacing rule for symbols. -3, !ready, member access, calls, and type punctuation follow their own grammar.

5. Function bodies always flush to the left

Parameters sit under the declaration header; the function body returns to the left margin.

  • Signature indentation: Group the inputs under their function.
  • Body at the margin: The divider and declaration establish ownership.
-- price-label(3, 20)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ price-label String
    - count Int
    - unit-price Int

"Total: ${count * unit-price}"

Compare the notation:

def price_label(count, unit_price):
    return f"Total: {count * unit_price}"

Why I chose it

  • I want indentation to express structure inside the body: branches, nested expressions, and block arguments.
  • Methods do not lose another level of horizontal space merely because they belong to a type.
  • Moving work between a module function and a method can preserve its visual shape.

Tradeoffs

  • Readers accustomed to indented bodies may initially mistake this for module-level code.
  • Dividers must make ownership clear. Control-flow blocks still rely on indentation.

6. One argument per line

Each ordinary declared parameter gets a line. Longer calls can use a matching block form.

  • Block call: Give each supplied argument a line.
  • Parameter outline: Keep each name and type together in a consistent column.
-- address-label
    - "Ada"
    - "10 Main Street"
    - "Honolulu"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ address-label String
    - recipient String
    - street String
    - city String

"$recipient, $street, $city"

Compare the notation:

function addressLabel(recipient: String, street: String, city: String): String

Compact calls such as address-label("Ada", "10 Main Street", "Honolulu") remain available. The line-per-argument form is an option at call sites.

Why I chose it

  • I want signatures to scan downward, with room for each name, type, and default.
  • A parameter change tends to produce a small, localized diff.

Tradeoffs

  • Tiny functions can spend more lines on their signatures than their bodies.
  • Vertical layout does not explain the roles of three positional strings. Named arguments solve that separate problem.

7. Prefer symbols over keywords

Small, recurring grammatical roles often use symbols. Pipelines make that preference especially visible.

  • Expand input: Contribute a range to the stream.
  • Filter: Keep values above two.
  • Transform: Produce 30, 40, 50.
. values = List
    ** 1 .. 5
    ?> each > 2
    *> each * 10
-- values

Compare the notation:

let values = range(1, 6)
    .filter(item => item > 2)
    .map(item => item * 10);
Yumi formConventional role
. value = ...Local binding
.. value = ...Lazy binding
+ name / - parameterPublic declaration / ordinary parameter
= value in a procedurereturn value
<= value in a generatoryield value
<<= valuesyield from values

This is a preference, not a ban on keywords: match, if, for, and do still have jobs.

Why I chose it

  • Once learned, the marks let me scan the shape of the work from its left edge.
  • I want repeated grammar to occupy less attention than the expressions it organizes.

Tradeoffs

  • Words such as filter give newcomers clues that ?> does not.
  • Symbols are harder to search for or say aloud, and assistive tools may read them inconsistently.
  • Familiar marks gain contextual meanings: statement-leading <= value yields, while left <= right compares.

8. Expression functions

An expression function states its answer directly, with supporting calculations below it.

  • Answer first: The body shows the output's shape without return.
  • Explain below: Evaluate the named dependency when it is needed.
-- receipt(3, 20)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ receipt String
    - count Int
    - unit-price Int

"Total: $total"

.. total = count * unit-price

Compare the notation:

function receipt(count, unitPrice) {
    const total = count * unitPrice;
    return `Total: ${total}`;
}

Why I chose it

  • I want to see the returned record, text, or decision before its supporting calculations.
  • Lazy bindings let source order follow the explanation: read the answer, then look up its ingredients.
  • Expression functions should be a normal way to write code, not just a shorthand for tiny helpers.

Tradeoffs

  • Laziness changes evaluation timing. Reads of mutable state and effects can make that difference observable.
  • An expression function is not a guarantee of purity.
  • do functions remain useful for mutation, cleanup, and early exits with =. Readers learn two body shapes.

9. Named arguments

A bullet passes an argument by the name of its parameter, so a call can state the role of each input.

  • Visible relationships: The call states which input is the origin and which is the destination.
  • Ordinary parameters: from and to are plain parameter names, used by the call and by the body.
-- travel • from "home" • to "office"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ travel String
    - from String
    - to String

"$from -> $to"

Compare the notation:

travel("home", "office")
travel(origin="home", destination="office")

Why I chose it

  • Named arguments make roles explicit, and relationship words such as from and to read well as parameter names.
  • They help when two inputs share a type and swapping them would still type-check.
  • Every named argument has one shape, • name value, whether it holds a value or a callback.

Tradeoffs

  • A parameter has one name, used both at the call site and in the body.
  • Vague names such as with can still make a poor API.
  • The bullets on a line all belong to one call, so a nested call takes its bullets inside parentheses.

10. Named infix operators

A two-input function can appear between its operands when its name is surrounded by slashes.

  • Infix call: Place a named relationship between its inputs.
  • Ordinary call: Use the same function with conventional call syntax; both print 7.
-- 3 /plus/ 4
-- plus(3, 4)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ plus Int
    - left Int
    - right Int

left + right

Compare the notation:

left ///combine/// middle /adjust/ right
left ///combine/// (middle /adjust/ right)
FormRelative precedence
/name/Highest of the named forms
//name//Middle
///name///Lowest

All bind less tightly than ordinary addition and multiplication. Slash count belongs to the call, not the function name. Alternatives include combine(left, right) and left.combine(right).

Why I chose it

  • I want left-to-right relationships without making an unmarked word ambiguous between operand and operator.
  • A domain operation can use an existing name without inventing a punctuation character. Bitwise operations use forms such as flags /and/ mask.

Tradeoffs

  • Readers must notice slash count to understand precedence. Domain vocabulary does not automatically make a long expression clear.
  • I would use parentheses whenever grouping deserves attention, or keep the ordinary call when it is clearer.

11. Parameterized types with apostrophes

Apostrophes attach type arguments to the type name.

  • Apply a type: Supply Int for the type parameter.
  • Declare a parameter: Item names the type used by the field.
. box = Box'Int(42)
-- box.value

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Box'Item is Tuple

+ value Item
YumiCommon angle-bracket spelling
Box'IntBox<Int>
Map'String'IntMap<String, Int>
List'(List'Int)List<List<Int>>

Square-bracket application, such as Box[Int], is another common alternative.

Why I chose it

  • A common short application needs no closing delimiter.
  • Flat argument lists avoid accumulating commas and angle brackets.
  • Apostrophes leave angle brackets available for streams and comparisons.

Tradeoffs

  • Nested applications need grouping, and a long chain of apostrophes can become hard to scan.
  • Copying must preserve the ASCII apostrophe rather than turn it into a typographic quote.
  • This simplifies a spelling, not generic inference or constraints.

12. Imports are bare paths

Dependencies appear as bare paths at the top of a file.

  • Library lookup: An absolute module path, not an operating-system root directory.
  • Relative lookup: A module near the current file.
/time/duration
./helpers

Conventional alternatives include import time.duration or import "./helpers".

Why I chose it

  • I want the dependency list to look like a list of dependencies, without a repeated keyword.
  • Slash notation keeps hierarchy and relative references visible.

Tradeoffs

  • The spelling borrows filesystem expectations, even though library lookup gives an absolute module path its meaning.
  • Removing import removes an obvious newcomer clue and a token that generic search tools can recognize.

The choices as a whole

These choices are easier to explain together than in isolation. Dividers support flush-left bodies. Hyphenated names depend on meaningful spaces around operators. Parameter lines and named arguments give calls an outline. Expression functions put the result first, while symbols keep the recurring scaffolding compact.

There is a tension in that design: I spend lines generously and characters selectively. I want a file to have enough visible structure to navigate, while keeping each expression's main content close together.

I also know that every departure from convention spends some of the reader's patience. Consistency does not erase that initial cost, and taste is not a substitute for observing where people struggle. My hope is that, once the vocabulary is familiar, the choices work together well enough that reading Yumi feels simpler than the list of rules makes it sound.

Features you may not like

Some things about Yumi take time to get used to. Others may be things you understand perfectly well and still disagree with. This page is about the second category.

These are choices with consequences for how you structure programs, reason about execution, and manage resources. Learning the notation does not make their tradeoffs disappear. I chose them because they support the kind of programming I want Yumi to make comfortable, but they also make Yumi less suitable for some preferences and requirements.

At a glance

Choice areaWhat may influence your decision
Source structureSignificant indentation and executable module bodies.
Type behaviorImplicit conversion, inferred signatures, operator overloading, multiple dispatch.
Object modelGarbage collection, inheritance, and virtual methods.
Control flowOrdinary calls can wait or propagate recoverable errors.

1. Python-like significant indentation

Indentation determines block structure. Moving a line can change behavior.

  • Conditional work: The indented print runs only when ready is true.
  • Following work: This prints regardless. Indenting it would make it conditional too.
. ready = false
if ready
    -- "Starting"
-- "Finished"

Why I chose it

  • Indentation is already how I read nested code. I want the visual grouping to be the compiler's grouping.
  • Dividers establish declaration boundaries; indentation describes structure inside them.

Tradeoffs

  • Whitespace can be fragile to copy and harder to inspect than explicit closing delimiters.
  • Moving text and changing scope are closely connected. Formatting becomes part of correctness.
  • If closing delimiters are central to how you navigate, this removes something useful.

2. Implicit type conversion

A supported conversion can happen because an assignment or argument expects another type.

  • Source representation: Begin with an integer.
  • Implicit conversion: The destination asks for floating point. Printing it produces 3.000000.
. count Int = 3
. amount F64 = count
-- amount

Why I chose it

  • When types already know the relationship, repeated casts can obscure the operation I want to express.
  • Connected units are a useful case: a function can ask for seconds while a caller supplies milliseconds.

Tradeoffs

  • Yumi permits narrowing as well as widening. Representation changes can lose precision.
  • Custom conversions can perform work that the assignment does not visibly announce.
  • API authors should reserve implicit conversions for predictable relationships; technical convertibility is not enough.

3. Garbage collection

Managed object memory uses garbage collection. Ordinary references do not require every caller to specify exactly who frees an object.

Managed automaticallyStill a program decision
Reclamation of managed object memoryHow long references remain reachable
Ordinary sharing of managed referencesWhen a socket, file, or subscription should stop
Collector-owned allocationsLifetimes of arenas, raw pointers, and native allocations

See memory choices and the cleanup example.

Why I chose it

  • I want sharing and object relationships to be ordinary: parent links, callbacks retaining objects, and several components referring to the same state.
  • Automating memory reclamation avoids making every relationship an ownership-design problem.

Tradeoffs

  • The collector uses runtime work and memory, and reclamation need not coincide with an object's last useful moment.
  • Strict latency or memory requirements can make that default unsuitable.
  • Reachable objects can retain unwanted memory. Files, locks, native allocations, and other resources still require deliberate lifetimes.

4. Operator overloading

Types can define operators for their values.

  • Domain expression: Add two offsets with ordinary arithmetic spelling.
  • Type-defined operator: Offset owns this meaning of addition.
  • Implementation: Combine coordinates, producing 6 and 8.
. combined = Offset(2, 3) + Offset(4, 5)
-- combined.x
-- combined.y

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Offset is Tuple

+ x Int
+ y Int

────────────────────
+ this + other Offset

Offset(x + other.x, y + other.y)

Why I chose it

  • Coordinates and quantities have established mathematical forms. I want expressions to preserve the shape of those calculations.

Tradeoffs

  • a + b can allocate, traverse data, or invoke domain behavior; the symbol does not state cost.
  • An inappropriate overload misleads readers. I expect + to mean a recognizable addition or combination.
  • Use a named function when the operation needs information its symbol cannot carry.

5. Multiple dispatch

An implementation can depend on more than one argument's type rather than one distinguished receiver.

  • Shared operation name: The calls produce 5 and Yumi!.
  • Numeric combination: Declare the implementation for two integer inputs.
  • Text combination: Declare the implementation for two strings. These concrete calls do not require runtime selection.
-- combine(2, 3)
-- combine("Yumi", "!")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ combine Int
    - left Int
    - right Int

left + right

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ combine String
    - left String
    - right String

left + right

Why I chose it

  • Combining values, converting representations, and handling interactions can naturally concern several participants.
  • Separate definitions describe the relevant combinations without making one type own every decision.

Tradeoffs

  • Finding the called implementation may require argument types, visible overloads, and dispatch rules.
  • New overloads can change selection or introduce ambiguity; implicit conversions add another consideration.
  • This is less local than a single receiver. Good diagnostics, navigation, and restrained API design matter.

6. Async functions are not “colored”

“Function coloring” separates async declarations and awaited calls from ordinary ones. Yumi allows suspension through ordinary calls. This fragment assumes /net/http and a URL named url.

  • Caller: Print the returned body using an ordinary call.
  • Helper: The declaration needs no async marker.
  • Network operation: The request can suspend; neither level needs await.
-- page-body(url)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ page-body String
    - url URL

page.text

.. page = http-get(url)

The request follows the repository's HTTP client example. See Concurrency and reactivity for the task model.

Why I chose it

  • I want to introduce helpers without propagating an asynchronous calling convention through every layer.
  • Sequential source remains useful for a sequence of operations even when execution waits between them.

Tradeoffs

  • The call site loses a visible suspension warning. Reconsider state observed before a wait and resources held across it.
  • Removing await does not make shared mutable state safe or make an operation atomic.
  • It also does not make every native blocking call cooperate with the scheduler. Timing remains part of the API contract.

7. Errors propagate automatically

A fallible call propagates errors unless a caller chooses a handling policy.

  • Declared error: The signature exposes the possible escaping failure.
  • Ordinary-looking call: Add on success; otherwise propagate without a call-site marker.
  • Recovery policy: Discard the error details, then replace absence with zero. This call prints 0.
-- catch? adjusted-count(false) ?? 0

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ CountFailure is Error

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ do read-count Int ?! CountFailure
    - available Bool

if available
    = 41
?! CountFailure("unavailable")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ adjusted-count Int ?! CountFailure
    - available Bool

read-count(available) + 1

Why I chose it

  • Many callers can only pass an error along. Repeating that instruction can overwhelm the calculation.
  • I want handling to stand out where a caller can recover, add context, or inspect the outcome.

Tradeoffs

  • An ordinary call does not announce a possible early exit. Explicit checking or propagation markers make that fact more local.
  • A fallback is a domain decision: zero must actually be acceptable for an unavailable count.
  • Propagation does not undo earlier mutations. Cleanup and partial progress still need design.

8. Class inheritance and virtual methods

Classes can inherit behavior and override methods selected according to the actual object.

  • Base-typed reference: The variable is declared as Greeting.
  • Virtual behavior: The actual object supplies the implementation.
  • Specialization: The override returns Welcome.
. greeting Greeting = FriendlyGreeting()
-- greeting.text()

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ Greeting

────────────────────
+ text String

"Hello"

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ FriendlyGreeting is Greeting

────────────────────
+ text String

"Welcome"

Why I chose it

  • Some families share a useful foundation of state and behavior.
  • Virtual methods keep the caller's contract common while allowing specialized behavior, without repetitive forwarding.

Tradeoffs

  • Behavior spreads across the hierarchy, and base decisions can constrain subclasses.
  • Changing shared behavior can affect distant code. A virtual call may reach a different implementation than the declared type suggests.
  • Composition, interfaces, and unions remain alternatives. Wanting a few methods is not enough reason to inherit.

9. Function parameter and return types can be inferred

Inference can apply at function boundaries as well as local bindings.

  • Concrete uses: Calls supply integer and string inputs.
  • Inferred boundary: The declaration omits parameter and return types while remaining statically typed.
-- identity(42)
-- identity("hello")

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ identity
    - value

value

Why I chose it

  • For small computations, annotations can duplicate what inputs and the result already establish.
  • Straightforward reusable helpers should not need repetitive type information everywhere.

Tradeoffs

  • An explicit signature is a readable contract and can constrain accidental interface changes.
  • Inference can make readers inspect the body or tooling, and a diagnostic may appear at a use site.
  • I still favor explicit types for public contracts, domain boundaries, and non-obvious results. The language permits inference; it does not require minimal signatures.

10. Executable code at module scope

A file can execute statements without wrapping them in a special entry-point function.

  • Start with the work: The module prints Hello, Yumi.
  • Add structure: The same file defines a reusable helper.
. name = "Yumi"
-- greeting(name)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
+ greeting String
    - name String

"Hello, $name"

Why I chose it

  • A small utility should begin with what it does; an entry-point wrapper need not be the first concept.
  • Functions and types can appear as the program needs structure.

Tradeoffs

  • A module is not necessarily passive: initialization can perform IO, change state, or fail.
  • Imports and startup dependencies become behavioral questions.
  • Substantial startup work benefits from named operations and deliberate sequencing; module code can be the small visible place that calls them.

What these choices ask of the reader

Several of these decisions let a short expression stand for behavior that another language would spell out at the call site. A conversion may be inserted, an implementation selected, a task suspended, or an error propagated. I want that support because repeated mechanical steps can make the program's purpose harder to see.

The corresponding obligation is that the behavior must remain discoverable. Types, declarations, documentation, diagnostics, and tools have to answer the questions that a short call expression leaves open. Concision is useful only when it does not turn necessary information into guesswork.

These tradeoffs will not suit everyone. I would rather explain what I chose and why than pretend that disagreement is only a matter of getting used to a new language.
